page.mentor_intro: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a medical emergency requiring rapid intervention to prevent irreversible visual loss. The IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab provides potent steroid-sparing immunosuppression, achieving sustained glucocorticoid-free remission in large-scale clinical trials.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark GiACTA randomized trial, subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg weekly or every other week) combined with a 26-week prednisone taper achieved significantly higher sustained glucocorticoid-free remission at 52 weeks (56% and 53%) compared with placebo plus 26-week (14%) or 52-week (18%) prednisone tapers (P<0.001).

Tocilizumab directly binds both soluble and membrane-bound interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptors, which rapidly normalizes acute-phase reactants (ESR and CRP) regardless of underlying persistent arterial wall inflammation, rendering ESR and CRP unreliable markers for disease flare during therapy.

Immediate high-dose glucocorticoid therapy (prednisolone 40-60 mg daily, or intravenous methylprednisolone pulses 500-1000 mg daily for 3 days if visual symptoms are present) must never be delayed while awaiting temporal artery biopsy or vascular ultrasound.

Routine safety monitoring during tocilizumab therapy requires periodic evaluation of neutrophil count, platelet count, liver transaminases, lipid profiles, and screening for latent tuberculosis and bowel perforation risk (diverticulitis history).

uncertainties: Optimal treatment duration with tocilizumab beyond 12 months and relapse rates following discontinuation.
Role of advanced imaging (PET-CT, contrast MRI) in monitoring persistent large-vessel vasculitis activity in patients with suppressed serum inflammatory markers.
mcq_angles: Biomarker unreliability during tocilizumab therapy: ESR and CRP remain suppressed due to IL-6 receptor blockade and cannot be used to monitor clinical relapse.
GiACTA trial clinical impact: proven steroid-sparing efficacy allowing cumulative prednisone reduction and sustained flare-free remission.
Pre-treatment screening: mandatory testing for latent tuberculosis and chronic hepatitis B/C, and assessing past history of diverticular disease.
case_hooks: A 72-year-old woman with biopsy-proven GCA experiencing recurrent jaw claudication and temporal headaches while tapering prednisone to 15 mg daily.
A 68-year-old man on tocilizumab 162 mg weekly for GCA who presents with fever and mild abdominal discomfort with normal CRP and ESR, subsequently found to have a perforated diverticulum.

page.mentor_intro: tonsillitis is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

teaching_points.claim: Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Tonsillectomy Versus Conservative Care for Recurrent or Chronic Tonsillitis in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Intracapsular Versus Extracapsular Tonsillectomy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

Acute tonsillitis is commonly viral, but Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) causes 15-30% of cases; clinical decision rules (Centor or FeverPAIN criteria) risk-stratify patients, with scores >=3 predicting streptococcal infection where oral phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) for 10 days shortens symptom duration by ~16 hours, prevents suppurative complications (peritonsillar abscess), and reduces transmission.

Sore throat decision rules (FeverPAIN score 4-5 or Centor 3-4) guide targeted antibiotic prescribing, where 10 days of oral penicillin V or clarithromycin accelerates symptom resolution and reduces transmission.

page.mentor_intro: Toxic and nutritional neuropathies present as insidious, length-dependent, symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathies. Recognizing deficiency states (B12, copper) and neurotoxic exposures (pyridoxine excess, platinum agents, taxanes) is essential for arresting axonal degeneration before permanent disability occurs.

teaching_points.claim: Nutritional and toxic neuropathies present with symmetric, length-dependent distal sensorimotor polyneuropathy; vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency characteristically produces subacute combined degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord, combining dorsal column sensory ataxia with lateral corticospinal tract spastic paraparesis.

While vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy, chronic excessive pyridoxine supplementation (>100-200 mg/day) produces severe, irreversible non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy (ganglionopathy) affecting dorsal root ganglia with profound sensory ataxia and areflexia.

Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a major dose-limiting complication of platinum compounds (oxaliplatin acute cold-induced dysesthesias; cisplatin cumulative sensory neuropathy), taxanes (paclitaxel axonal neuropathy), vinca alkaloids (vincristine autonomic and motor neuropathy), and proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib).

In patients with low-normal serum B12 levels (150-300 pmol/L), elevated functional metabolic intermediates—methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine—confirm true intracellular cobalamin deficiency; concurrent copper deficiency must be excluded as it closely mimics subacute combined degeneration.

uncertainties: Efficacy of duloxetine as the only guideline-recommended pharmacotherapy for symptomatic chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy.
Role of neurofilament light chain (NfL) biomarkers in detecting subclinical early axonal injury before irreversible neuropathy develops.
mcq_angles: Pyridoxine toxicity paradox: mega-dose vitamin B6 causes pure sensory ganglionopathy with loss of proprioception and preserved motor power.
Differential diagnosis of subacute combined degeneration: copper deficiency (e.g., from zinc toxicity or gastric bypass) produces identical posterior/lateral column degeneration.
Oxaliplatin unique toxicity: acute cold-triggered perioral and distal paresthesias occurring during or immediately following infusion.

page.mentor_intro: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) represent life-threatening, immune-mediated mucocutaneous reactions characterized by extensive keratinocyte apoptosis, epidermal detachment, and severe mucosal ulceration. SJS/TEN is classified by the body surface area (BSA) of epidermal detachment: SJS (<10%), SJS/TEN overlap (10-30%), and TEN (>30%). Over 80-90% of TEN cases are triggered by medications (allopurinol, aromatic antiseizure medications [carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine], sulfonamide antimicrobials, nevirapine, and oxicam NSAIDs); prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug and immediate transfer to a specialized burn center or intensive care unit are paramount.

teaching_points.claim: Immediate identification and cessation of the culprit drug is the single most critical intervention; delay in discontinuing long half-life culprit medications significantly increases mortality.

The SCORTEN prognostic score (incorporating age >=40, heart rate >=120 bpm, malignancy, epidermal detachment >10% BSA, serum urea >10 mmol/L, glucose >14 mmol/L, bicarbonate <20 mmol/L) calculated within the first 24 hours accurately predicts in-hospital mortality.

Supportive ICU/burn care forms the foundation: protective barrier care, warmed environment (30-32 C) to prevent hypothermia, meticulous fluid and electrolyte resuscitation, non-adherent silicone dressings without surgical debridement, and aggressive ophthalmic lubrication and daily release of conjunctival adhesions with amniotic membrane transplantation.

Targeted immunomodulatory therapies—prominently cyclosporine (3-5 mg/kg daily) and the TNF inhibitor etanercept (50 mg SC)—halt cytotoxic T-cell/granulysin-mediated keratinocyte apoptosis and reduce mortality compared to historical IVIG or high-dose corticosteroids.

uncertainties: Comparative survival benefit of cyclosporine versus etanercept as first-line monotherapy in severe TEN.
Role of prophylactic HLA-B*1502 and HLA-B*5801 pharmacogenetic screening in diverse multi-ethnic populations to eliminate antiepileptic and allopurinol-induced SJS/TEN.
mcq_angles: Calculating the SCORTEN score on day 1 to predict mortality and guide ICU triage.
Distinguishing SJS (<10% BSA detachment), SJS/TEN overlap (10-30%), and TEN (>30% BSA).
Urgent ophthalmic management: mandatory daily ophthalmology consultation and early amniotic membrane transplantation to prevent blinding cicatricial symblepharon.
case_hooks: A 42-year-old male recently initiated on allopurinol develops painful oral mucosal erosions, purpuric macules with positive Nikolsky sign, and 35% BSA epidermal sloughing (TEN); SCORTEN is 3.
A child on lamotrigine presents with hemorrhagic crusting of the lips, bilateral severe conjunctival injection, and widespread flaccid bullae across the chest and back.

page.mentor_intro: Tracheobronchomalacia (TBM) is a pathological condition characterized by dynamic structural weakness and excessive collapsibility of the tracheal and bronchial cartilaginous rings and posterior membranous wall during expiration. It is classified into congenital (primary) forms in infants—often linked to tracheoesophageal fistula or prematurity—and acquired (secondary) forms in adults, triggered by chronic airway inflammation (COPD, relapsing polychondritis), prolonged endotracheal intubation, or trauma. Dynamic flexible bronchoscopy during active forced expiration or coughing is the gold standard for definitive diagnosis, identifying >=50% (and often >=70-80%) dynamic airway lumen collapse.

teaching_points.claim: Definitive diagnosis of tracheobronchomalacia requires dynamic flexible bronchoscopy during tidal breathing, deep expiration, and forced coughing, documenting >=50% reduction in luminal cross-sectional area (with severe disease defined as >=70-80% collapse).

Dynamic multi-detector paired inspiratory-expiratory computed tomography (dynamic CT) serves as the primary non-invasive imaging modality of choice, capturing the 'frown sign' of dynamic crescentic airway narrowing on end-expiratory phases.

Conservative medical management includes non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP), which acts as a 'pneumatic stent' to maintain dynamic airway patency during exhalation, paired with aggressive pulmonary clearance and treatment of underlying COPD.

In severe, highly symptomatic adult TBM refractory to conservative therapy, surgical tracheobronchoplasty (posterior membranous wall stabilization using polypropylene mesh, performed open or robotic-assisted) provides durable symptomatic and functional improvement following a successful temporary stent trial.

uncertainties: Long-term complication rates (granulation tissue, stent migration, mucus plugging) of silicone versus self-expanding metallic stents in adult central airway collapse.
Efficacy and patient selection for posterior tracheopexy versus aortopexy in paediatric severe tracheomalacia.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic gold standard for TBM: dynamic flexible bronchoscopy during forced expiration or coughing.
Pneumatic stenting mechanism: explaining how continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) prevents dynamic expiratory collapse.
Preoperative evaluation for surgical tracheobronchoplasty: utility of a temporary silicone or metallic Y-stent trial to confirm symptomatic reversibility.
case_hooks: A 62-year-old male with severe COPD and recurrent lower respiratory infections presents with a harsh, barking ('seal-like') cough and inability to clear secretions; dynamic expiratory CT reveals 85% collapse of the distal trachea and both mainstem bronchi.
An 8-month-old infant with a history of repaired esophageal atresia presents with persistent stridor, barking cough, and recurrent reflex apnoeic spells ('dying spells') during feeding.

page.mentor_intro: Tracheostomy is one of the most common surgical procedures performed in critically ill patients requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation, acute airway obstruction, or chronic pulmonary toilet impairment. Timing of tracheostomy—traditionally categorized into early (within 7-10 days) versus late (>10-14 days)—balances the risks of prolonged translaryngeal intubation (glottic injury, subglottic stenosis) against procedural complications and unnecessary operations in rapidly weaning patients. Percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy (PDT) performed at the bedside in the ICU has largely superseded open surgical tracheostomy (OST) for elective adult patients due to reduced wound infections and comparable safety when guided by real-time bronchoscopy.

teaching_points.claim: Major indications for tracheostomy in the ICU include: anticipated prolonged mechanical ventilation, failed extubation, severe neurological deficit with loss of protective airway reflexes, and acute or chronic upper airway obstruction.

The landmark TracMan trial demonstrated that early tracheostomy (within day 4) does not improve 30-day or 1-year mortality compared to late tracheostomy (after day 10), but significantly reduces the duration of sedation and ICU length of stay.

Percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy (PDT) at the bedside is associated with lower surgical site infection rates, smaller incisions, less tissue trauma, and reduced hospital costs compared to open surgical tracheostomy, provided anatomical contraindications are absent.

Real-time bronchoscopic visualization during percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy significantly reduces catastrophic procedural complications, including posterior tracheal wall laceration, paratracheal false-passage placement, and pneumothorax.

uncertainties: Optimal timing of tracheostomy in acute cervical spinal cord injury (day 3-5 vs later) to prevent pulmonary complications and facilitate diaphragm weaning.
Standardized protocols for decannulation readiness using peak cough flow, blue dye testing, and capping trials in ICU survivors.
mcq_angles: TracMan trial findings: early vs late tracheostomy impact on mortality (no difference) vs sedation requirements and ICU stay (improved with early).

Anatomical contraindications to bedside percutaneous tracheostomy favoring open surgical tracheostomy (morbid obesity with unidentifiable landmarks, gross thyroid goitre, cervical spine instability, severe coagulopathy).
Role of continuous bronchoscopic guidance during percutaneous dilational tracheostomy.
case_hooks: A 52-year-old male with severe traumatic brain injury remains comatose (GCS 6) on mechanical ventilation on day 8; the ICU team plans elective tracheostomy for airway protection and weaning.
During a bedside percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy, the intensivist utilizes dynamic bronchoscopy to guide needle puncture between the second and third tracheal cartilages.

page.mentor_intro: Damage control resuscitation (DCR) is the modern paradigm for resuscitating severe trauma patients with life-threatening haemorrhagic shock, targeting the lethal triad of coagulopathy, hypothermia, and acidosis. DCR integrates permissive hypotension (MAP ~50-65 mmHg pending surgical haemostasis), balanced blood component transfusion ratios (1:1:1 of packed RBCs, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets), and early antifibrinolytic therapy. Tranexamic acid (TXA)—a synthetic lysine analogue that competitively blocks plasminogen activation—was proven by the CRASH-2 trial to reduce trauma mortality when administered within 3 hours of injury, while administration after 3 hours increases mortality.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark CRASH-2 trial demonstrated that early administration of tranexamic acid (1 g IV bolus over 10 minutes followed by 1 g IV infusion over 8 hours) significantly reduces all-cause mortality and death due to bleeding in trauma patients with significant haemorrhage.
Tranexamic acid must be administered within 3 hours of injury; administration after 3 hours is associated with increased bleeding-related mortality and is strictly contraindicated.

Damage control resuscitation prioritizes balanced 1:1:1 transfusion ratios of packed red blood cells, plasma, and platelets, minimizing large-volume crystalloid infusions to prevent dilutional coagulopathy and endothelial glycocalyx disruption (PROPPR trial).

In patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), the CRASH-3 trial demonstrated that TXA reduces head injury-related death in mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS 9-15) when given within 3 hours of trauma, with negligible benefit in severe TBI (GCS 3-8).

uncertainties: Efficacy and vascular thromboembolism risks of pre-hospital TXA administration versus in-hospital administration (PATCH-Trauma trial findings).
Individualized viscoelastometric testing (TEG / ROTEM) guided TXA dosing versus standardized empiric 2 g bolus protocols.
mcq_angles: CRASH-2 timing rule: explaining why TXA must be given within 3 hours of trauma injury and why post-3-hour administration increases mortality.
Dosing regimen of TXA in trauma resuscitation: 1 g IV loading dose over 10 minutes, followed by 1 g IV infusion over 8 hours.
Damage control resuscitation components: permissive hypotension, 1:1:1 transfusion ratio, and limitation of crystalloids.
case_hooks: A 28-year-old male sustains multiple gunshot wounds to the abdomen, presenting 45 minutes post-injury with BP 74/42 mmHg, HR 135 bpm, and massive external haemorrhage; the trauma team initiates the massive transfusion protocol and TXA bolus.

page.mentor_intro: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)—traditionally defined as blood loss >=500 mL following vaginal delivery or >=1000 mL following caesarean delivery—is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide. Following delivery, separation of the placenta activates physiological tissue factor release, which is rapidly followed by local and systemic hyperfibrinolysis that exacerbates coagulopathic bleeding. The landmark WOMAN trial established that early administration of intravenous tranexamic acid (TXA) reduces death due to bleeding by nearly one-third when given within 3 hours of birth, while administration after 3 hours provides no benefit.

teaching_points.claim: The WOMAN trial demonstrated that intravenous tranexamic acid (1 g IV over 10 minutes) significantly reduces death due to bleeding by 31% when administered within 3 hours of delivery (RR 0.69, p = 0.008), with a second 1 g dose if bleeding continues after 30 minutes.

Tranexamic acid must be administered as early as possible after PPH diagnosis; treatment initiated after 3 hours of birth provides zero survival benefit, reflecting the critical window of early hyperfibrinolytic coagulopathy.

TXA should be administered alongside standard first-line uterotonic agents (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol) and surgical/tamponade interventions; it does not increase maternal thromboembolic events (DVT, PE, or stroke).

Prophylactic tranexamic acid administered immediately prior to high-risk caesarean section (e.g., in placenta praevia, multiple gestation, repeat caesarean) significantly reduces measured intraoperative blood loss and need for transfusion (TRAAP2 trial).

uncertainties: Efficacy and pharmacokinetic bioavailability of intramuscular, oral, or sublingual tranexamic acid formulations in resource-constrained community birth settings.
Role of viscoelastometric testing (ROTEM/TEG) in guiding fibrinogen concentrate versus cryoprecipitate replacement alongside TXA in severe amniotic fluid embolism-induced PPH.
mcq_angles: Timing window from the WOMAN trial: explaining why TXA must be administered within 3 hours of birth for postpartum haemorrhage.
Standard dosing of TXA in PPH: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, with a repeat 1 g dose if bleeding persists after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours.
Thromboembolic safety of TXA in obstetric populations (no increased risk of venous thromboembolism).
case_hooks: A 28-year-old primigravida sustains an atonic postpartum haemorrhage of 1,200 mL 45 minutes following an uncomplicated vaginal delivery; the obstetrician administers oxytocin infusion, bimanual uterine compression, and IV tranexamic acid 1 g.

A patient undergoing repeat caesarean section for placenta praevia receives prophylactic IV tranexamic acid 1 g at umbilical cord clamping, significantly decreasing postoperative transfusion requirements.

page.mentor_intro: Severe trauma hemorrhage triggers early acute coagulopathy of trauma (ACOT), driven by tissue hypoperfusion, endothelial glycocalyx breakdown, and massive systemic hyperfibrinolysis. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is a synthetic lysine analogue that competitively binds the lysine-binding sites of plasminogen, preventing its activation into plasmin and halting fibrin clot degradation. The landmark CRASH-2 trial revolutionized trauma resuscitation globally, proving that early TXA administration reduces all-cause and bleeding mortality without increasing vascular occlusive events.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark CRASH-2 trial (20,211 trauma patients across 40 countries) established that tranexamic acid administered as a 1 g IV loading dose over 10 minutes followed by 1 g IV infusion over 8 hours significantly reduced all-cause mortality (14.5% vs 16.0%, p = 0.0035) and bleeding death.

The mortality benefit of TXA is profoundly time-dependent: administration within 1 hour of injury reduces risk of death from bleeding by 32%; administration between 1 and 3 hours reduces bleeding death by 21%; whereas administration after 3 hours INCREASES the risk of death due to bleeding (RR 1.44, p = 0.004).
Tranexamic acid administration in CRASH-2 did not increase the incidence of fatal or non-fatal vascular occlusive events (myocardial infarction, stroke, pulmonary embolism, DVT).

In patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), the CRASH-3 trial demonstrated that TXA within 3 hours reduces head injury-related mortality in mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS 9-15), with greatest benefit seen when administered within the first 2 hours.

uncertainties: Pre-hospital empiric TXA administration in all severe trauma versus targeted in-hospital administration guided by rapid rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) clot lysis (PATCH-Trauma trial).
Optimal dosing strategies (single 2 g IV bolus vs the standard 1 g + 1 g 8-hour infusion) in military and civilian aeromedical evacuation.
mcq_angles: The critical 3-hour cutoff: why TXA administered >3 hours post-trauma is harmful and contraindicated.
CRASH-2 dosing protocol: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g IV infused over 8 hours.
CRASH-3 findings in traumatic brain injury: survival benefit restricted to mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS 9-15) treated within 3 hours.
case_hooks: A 32-year-old male sustains severe pelvic and femoral fractures in a car crash; emergency medical services arrive at minute 35 and immediately infuse a 1 g IV bolus of tranexamic acid.

A trauma patient arrives in the resuscitation bay 3.5 hours post-injury; the surgical team recognizes that TXA should not be initiated due to the harmful late-administration mortality signal in CRASH-2.

page.mentor_intro: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI, or TAVR) has revolutionized the treatment of severe symptomatic native aortic stenosis across prohibitive, high, intermediate, and low surgical risk patients. Multidisciplinary 'Heart Team' evaluation integrates anatomical suitability on ECG-gated multidetector CT (annulus dimensions, coronary ostial heights, calcification distribution, and transfemoral access caliber) with clinical risk scores (STS, EuroSCORE II) and patient life expectancy. Although transfemoral TAVI achieves outstanding hemodynamics and rapid recovery, operators must anticipate and manage specific complications: high-degree atrioventricular conduction block requiring permanent pacemaker, paravalvular regurgitation, vascular access injury, and stroke.

teaching_points.claim: Transfemoral access is the preferred first-line vascular approach for TAVI (>90% of cases), requiring minimum iliofemoral luminal diameters (typically >=5.0-5.5 mm depending on sheath size) without circumferential calcification or severe tortuosity.

Pre-procedural ECG-gated multislice cardiac CT is mandatory to measure the aortic valve annulus area/perimeter, evaluate coronary artery take-off heights (distance <10-12 mm from annulus confers risk of acute coronary ostial obstruction), and plan coplanar fluoroscopic angles.

New-onset high-degree atrioventricular block and permanent pacemaker (PPM) implantation remain frequent complications, occurring more often with self-expanding valves (15-25%) than balloon-expandable valves (5-10%), due to mechanical compression of the membranous septum and His bundle.

Paravalvular aortic regurgitation (PVL)—arising from incomplete frame sealing in heavily calcified commissures—is associated with increased long-term mortality and is classified by VARC-3 criteria using Doppler echocardiography.

uncertainties: Long-term structural valve deterioration (SVD) and durability of transcatheter bioprostheses beyond 10 years compared to surgical bioprosthetic valves.
Optimal antithrombotic therapy post-TAVI in patients without baseline anticoagulation indications (single antiplatelet therapy [SAPT] with aspirin vs DAPT vs oral anticoagulants).
mcq_angles: Identifying risk factors for acute coronary ostial obstruction during TAVI (coronary height <10-12 mm and shallow sinuses of Valsalva).
Predictors and rates of permanent pacemaker requirement comparing self-expanding vs balloon-expandable prostheses.

Patient selection: transcatheter versus surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) in younger low-risk patients (<65-70 years) where valve durability, bicuspid anatomy, and lifetime coronary access are primary concerns.
case_hooks: An 82-year-old female with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (mean gradient 48 mmHg, valve area 0.6 cm2) and STS score 6.2% is evaluated for transfemoral TAVI; CT shows coronary ostia at 14 mm and femoral arteries measuring 6.5 mm.

Following successful deployment of a self-expanding transcatheter aortic valve, a patient develops new right bundle branch block with first-degree AV block and intermittent 2:1 Mobitz II block on telemetry.

page.mentor_intro: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) was initially developed for inoperable and high-surgical-risk patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, but has rapidly expanded into intermediate- and low-risk cohorts. The landmark PARTNER 3 randomized trial evaluated balloon-expandable TAVR (using the SAPIEN 3 prosthesis) versus surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) in low-surgical-risk patients (STS score <4%). PARTNER 3 established that balloon-expandable TAVR was superior to surgery at 1 year for the primary composite endpoint of death, stroke, or rehospitalization, establishing transfemoral TAVR as a standard alternative to open heart surgery across all surgical risk tiers.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark PARTNER 3 trial demonstrated that balloon-expandable TAVR in low-surgical-risk patients (mean STS score 1.9%) was superior to surgery, achieving a significant 46% reduction in the primary composite endpoint of death, stroke, or rehospitalization at 1 year (8.5% vs 15.1%, p < 0.001 for superiority).

Balloon-expandable TAVR in low-risk patients resulted in shorter index hospital stays (mean 3 days vs 7 days), lower new-onset atrial fibrillation (5.0% vs 39.5%), and faster recovery of physical function and quality of life compared to surgical valve replacement.

New left bundle branch block (LBBB, ~15-20%) and permanent pacemaker implantation (~6-7% with balloon-expandable valves) remain more frequent after TAVR than SAVR, requiring continuous ECG monitoring and structured post-procedure telemetry protocols.

Long-term Heart Team decision-making in young low-risk patients (<65-70 years) must weigh valve durability beyond 10 years, lifetime coronary re-access through the stent frame, bicuspid aortic valve morphology, and the feasibility of future TAVR-in-TAVR versus surgical explantation.

uncertainties: Structural valve deterioration (SVD) and bioprosthetic valve failure rates of balloon-expandable transcatheter valves beyond 10-15 years in younger cohorts.
Optimal antithrombotic strategy post-TAVR in low-risk patients without baseline anticoagulation indications (aspirin monotherapy versus short-term DAPT).
mcq_angles: PARTNER 3 trial primary outcomes: superiority of balloon-expandable TAVR over SAVR at 1 year for death, stroke, or rehospitalization in low-risk patients.
Complication tradeoffs: lower rate of atrial fibrillation and bleeding with TAVR vs higher rate of new conduction abnormalities (LBBB, pacemaker) and mild paravalvular leak.
Lifetime management considerations: assessing coronary ostial height and sinus dimensions for future valve-in-valve procedures.
case_hooks: A 72-year-old active retired engineer with severe symptomatic calcific aortic stenosis (mean gradient 46 mmHg, valve area 0.7 cm2) and STS score of 1.4% undergoes multidisciplinary Heart Team evaluation and elects transfemoral SAPIEN 3 TAVR.
Following successful balloon-expandable TAVR, an asymptomatic patient develops new persistent LBBB with QRS duration 150 ms, requiring prolonged 48-hour telemetry monitoring.

page.mentor_intro: Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO) is an acute, hydrostatic pulmonary oedema precipitated by the transfusion of blood products, and represents the leading cause of transfusion-related morbidity and mortality in high-income countries. Pathophysiology involves excessive volume, rapid infusion rate, or impaired cardiovascular/renal compensation, leading to elevated left atrial pressures and fluid extravasation into lung alveoli. Differentiating TACO from Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI)—which is non-cardiogenic and mediated by neutrophil activation—is critical, as TACO responds dramatically to diuresis and positive pressure ventilation whereas TRALI does not.

teaching_points.claim: TACO is defined clinically by acute respiratory distress developing within 6 (or up to 12) hours of blood product transfusion, with evidence of hydrostatic cardiac overload (tachycardia, hypertension, elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly/pulmonary oedema on CXR, and marked elevation in BNP or NT-proBNP).
Major risk factors for TACO include advanced age (>70 years), pre-existing congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease, hypoalbuminaemia, rapid infusion rates, and large-volume transfusion.

TACO is distinguished from TRALI by the presence of systemic hypertension (versus hypotension in TRALI), elevated jugular venous pressure, responsive diuresis with loop diuretics, and post-transfusion BNP elevation >1.5-fold baseline.

Prevention requires pre-transfusion risk assessment, restrictive single-unit red cell transfusion strategies, slowing infusion rates (transfusing a single unit over 3 to 4 hours), and prophylactic pre- or mid-transfusion loop diuretics (e.g., IV furosemide 20-40 mg) in high-risk patients.

uncertainties: Diagnostic accuracy and specific cutoff thresholds for pre- versus post-transfusion NT-proBNP in differentiating mixed TACO/TRALI presentations.
Effectiveness of automated electronic health record clinical decision support alerts in prompting prophylactic diuretic orders for high-risk patients.
mcq_angles: Differentiating TACO from TRALI: hypertension, elevated JVP, high post-transfusion BNP/NT-proBNP, and rapid response to IV furosemide definitively favor TACO.
Immediate emergency management of suspected TACO: stop transfusion, sit patient upright, administer high-flow oxygen/CPAP, and give intravenous loop diuretics.
Prophylactic strategies for TACO in high-risk patients (pre-transfusion IV furosemide, single-unit transfusion over 3-4 hours).

page.mentor_intro: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is defined as a transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute tissue infarction on neuroimaging. TIA is a medical emergency: the risk of recurrent, disabling ischaemic stroke is highest in the first 48 to 72 hours (up to 5-10% at 48 hours and 10-20% at 90 days), with the majority of secondary strokes occurring within the first 24-48 hours. Immediate rapid assessment—utilizing the ABCD2 score, emergency brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), urgent vascular imaging of the carotid and vertebral arteries, and expedited secondary prevention—reduces 90-day stroke risk by over 80% (SOS-TIA and EXPRESS studies).

teaching_points.claim: The ABCD2 score stratifies early stroke risk after TIA: Age >=60 (1 pt), Blood pressure >=140/90 (1 pt), Clinical features (unilateral weakness [2 pts], speech disturbance without weakness [1 pt]), Duration (>=60 min [2 pts], 10-59 min [1 pt]), and Diabetes (1 pt); scores >=4 represent high early stroke risk.

Emergency brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is the imaging modality of choice; approximately 30-40% of patients with transient symptoms lasting <24 hours demonstrate acute punctate ischemic infarctions on DWI, reclassifying them as true ischemic strokes with elevated recurrence risk.

Immediate non-invasive vascular imaging (carotid Doppler ultrasound, CT angiography, or MR angiography of neck and intracranial vessels) is mandatory to identify symptomatic carotid artery stenosis >=50-70%, which requires urgent carotid endarterectomy (CEA) ideally within 7 to 14 days.

Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT: aspirin 81-100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg with a 300-600 mg loading dose) initiated within 24 hours and continued for 21 days significantly reduces 90-day recurrent stroke in high-risk TIA (ABCD2 >=4) or minor stroke (NIHSS <=3) (CHANCE and POINT trials).

uncertainties: Efficacy of ticagrelor plus aspirin compared to clopidogrel plus aspirin in high-risk TIA patients with CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles (THALES trial insights).
Duration of outpatient cardiac rhythm monitoring (mobile cardiac telemetry vs insertable cardiac monitor) to detect occult paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in cryptogenic TIA.
mcq_angles: Calculating ABCD2 score and selecting candidates for 21-day DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) based on score >=4.
Time-critical referral for carotid endarterectomy: performing surgery within 7-14 days of transient symptoms in 70-99% symptomatic stenosis.
Diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) superiority over non-contrast CT in detecting acute microinfarction in transient symptoms.

page.mentor_intro: Transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE/TEE) provides high-resolution ultrasonic visualization of posterior cardiac structures unobstructed by chest wall, ribs, or lung parenchyma. Because the transducer sits in the mid-oesophagus directly posterior to the left atrium, TOE is the undisputed gold standard for detecting left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombi, ruling out infective endocarditis vegetations and perivalvular abscesses, and guiding transcatheter structural heart interventions. Safe performance demands pre-procedure evaluation of oesophageal pathology contraindications, conscious sedation monitoring, and multiplane probe manipulation.

teaching_points.claim: TOE is the gold standard modality for excluding left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombus prior to direct current cardioversion or catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation/flutter, exhibiting sensitivity and specificity approaching 99-100%.

In suspected infective endocarditis (IE), TOE is strongly indicated when transthoracic echo (TTE) is negative or non-diagnostic despite high clinical suspicion, in all patients with prosthetic valves or intracardiac devices, and to detect invasive perivalvular complications (root abscess, fistula, leaflet perforation).

Comprehensive prosthetic valve assessment by TOE evaluates mechanism of dysfunction (structural leaflet degeneration, pannus ingrowth vs mobile thrombus, paravalvular regurgitant jets, rocking of the sewing ring in dehiscence).

Absolute contraindications to TOE include oesophageal pathology with risk of perforation: oesophageal stricture, oesophageal carcinoma, active upper gastrointestinal bleeding, oesophageal perforation, Zenker diverticulum, and recent oesophageal surgery.

uncertainties: Diagnostic equivalence of modern 4D cardiac CT angiography compared to TOE for pre-procedural left atrial appendage thrombus exclusion.
Routine utility of TOE versus surface POCUS during active cardiopulmonary resuscitation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
mcq_angles: Mandatory TOE indications in infective endocarditis: prosthetic valves, intracardiac electronic devices, and suspected perivalvular abscess.
Excluding LAA thrombus before cardioversion: identifying 'smoke' (spontaneous echo contrast, a precursor of stasis) versus discrete mobile thrombus in the pectinate muscles.
Identifying absolute contraindications to TOE probe insertion (active GI bleeding, oesophageal malignancy/stricture, Zenker diverticulum).

page.mentor_intro: Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) is a progressive, fatal systemic protein-misfolding disorder caused by the dissociation of transthyretin tetramers into misfolded monomers that aggregate as insoluble amyloid fibrils in myocardial and neural tissues. ATTR manifests as ATTR cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) and/or ATTR polyneuropathy (ATTR-PN), occurring in both wild-type (ATTRwt, predominantly in older men) and hereditary variant (ATTRv) forms. The therapeutic landscape has undergone a revolutionary shift from purely supportive care to targeted disease-modifying therapies: kinetic tetramer stabilizers (tafamidis, acoramidis) and hepatic gene-silencing therapies (RNA interference: patisiran, vutrisiran; antisense oligonucleotides: inotersen, eplontersen).

teaching_points.claim: Tafamidis is a kinetic stabilizer that binds with high affinity to the thyroxine-binding sites of the TTR tetramer, preventing dissociation into amyloidogenic monomers; the landmark ATTR-ACT trial established that tafamidis reduces all-cause mortality by 30% and cardiovascular hospitalizations in ATTR cardiomyopathy.

Non-invasive diagnostic criteria for ATTR cardiomyopathy allow diagnosis without endomyocardial biopsy if patients have typical heart failure/echo findings, Grade 2 or 3 cardiac uptake on 99mTc-pyrophosphate (PYP) or DPND bone scintigraphy, AND completely negative serum/urine monoclonal protein studies (immunofixation and free light chains).

RNA interference (RNAi) therapeutics—specifically patisiran (IV every 3 weeks) and vutrisiran (subcutaneous every 3 months)—target hepatic TTR mRNA, degrading the transcript and reducing serum transthyretin production by >80-85%, halting or reversing polyneuropathy progression (APOLLO and HELIOS-A trials).

The HELIOS-B trial demonstrated that vutrisiran significantly reduces all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with ATTR cardiomyopathy, establishing subcutaneous gene silencers as potent disease-modifying agents in cardiac disease.

uncertainties: Long-term combination therapy: whether combining a TTR gene silencer (vutrisiran) with a tetramer stabilizer (tafamidis) provides additive clinical benefit over monotherapy.
Role of emerging in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing (e.g., nexiguran ziclumeran) in achieving permanent single-dose suppression of mutant and wild-type TTR.
mcq_angles: ATTR-ACT trial landmark findings: tafamidis reduces 30-month mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in ATTR-CM.
Non-invasive diagnosis requirements: positive 99mTc-PYP/DPD scan (grade 2-3) PLUS strict exclusion of AL amyloidosis via serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light chains.
Mechanism of action of gene silencers (vutrisiran, patisiran: mRNA degradation) versus stabilizers (tafamidis, acoramidis: tetramer stabilization).
case_hooks: A 76-year-old male presents with HFpEF, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, and low-voltage QRS on ECG despite marked concentric LV wall thickening (16 mm); 99mTc-PYP scan shows intense Grade 3 myocardial uptake with normal light chains.

A 54-year-old woman with confirmed hereditary ATTR (Val30Met mutation) presents with progressive sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy and orthostatic hypotension, evaluated for subcutaneous vutrisiran initiation.

page.mentor_intro: HER2-positive breast cancer—characterized by human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) gene amplification or protein overexpression—was historically associated with aggressive tumour biology, high recurrence rates, and poor survival. Trastuzumab is a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting the extracellular juxtamembrane domain IV of the HER2 receptor, inhibiting downstream MAPK and PI3K/Akt signaling, preventing receptor shedding, and mediating antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). The landmark BCIRG 006 trial established adjuvant trastuzumab as the transformative standard of care, while demonstrating that a non-anthracycline regimen (TCH: docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab) achieved equivalent disease-free and overall survival to anthracycline-based therapy with significantly less cardiotoxicity.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark BCIRG 006 trial demonstrated that 1 year of adjuvant trastuzumab combined with chemotherapy significantly improved 10-year disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) in early-stage HER2-positive breast cancer compared to chemotherapy alone.

BCIRG 006 compared AC-T (doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by docetaxel), AC-TH (AC-T plus trastuzumab), and TCH (docetaxel, carboplatin, and trastuzumab); TCH achieved identical survival to AC-TH with a significantly lower rate of symptomatic congestive heart failure (0.4% vs 2.0%, p = 0.001) and fewer secondary leukaemias.

Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity (Type II cardiotoxicity) is characterized by reversible, dose-independent myocardial dysfunction without ultrastructural myocyte necrosis, in contrast to cumulative, irreversible anthracycline cardiomyopathy (Type I cardiotoxicity); baseline and 3-monthly echocardiography (LVEF monitoring) is mandatory.

Standard adjuvant trastuzumab duration is 12 months; in modern practice, high-risk node-positive patients receive dual HER2 blockade (trastuzumab plus pertuzumab per APHINITY), while patients with residual invasive disease after neoadjuvant therapy are transitioned to trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1 per KATHERINE).

uncertainties: De-escalation strategies: whether 6 months of adjuvant trastuzumab is non-inferior to 12 months in selected low-risk small HER2-positive tumours (PHARE and Short-HER trials).
Role of upfront subcutaneous fixed-dose co-formulation (pertuzumab and trastuzumab with hyaluronidase-zzxf [Phesgo]) compared to sequential IV infusions.
mcq_angles: BCIRG 006 landmark findings: non-anthracycline TCH regimen provides equivalent survival to AC-TH with significantly lower cardiotoxicity.
Characteristics of trastuzumab cardiotoxicity (Type II: non-dose-dependent, usually reversible upon drug cessation) versus anthracycline cardiotoxicity (Type I: dose-dependent myocyte death).
KATHERINE trial standard of care: transitioning patients with residual invasive disease post-neoadjuvant therapy from trastuzumab to T-DM1.
case_hooks: A 48-year-old female with early HER2-positive breast cancer and a history of well-controlled hypertension is prescribed adjuvant TCH (docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab) to minimize anthracycline-related cardiac risk.
During cycle 6 of adjuvant trastuzumab, an asymptomatic patient's LVEF drops from 62% to 44%; trastuzumab is held, ACE inhibitor therapy is initiated, and LVEF recovers to 58% at 6 weeks.

page.mentor_intro: Modern trauma resuscitation has evolved from historical high-volume crystalloid infusion to physiological Damage Control Resuscitation (DCR), prioritizing rapid anatomical haemostasis and reversal of the trauma 'lethal triad' (hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, and trauma-induced coagulopathy). Resuscitation follows structured Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) and 'x-ABCDE' principles, elevating catastrophic external exsanguination ('x') to the immediate first priority. Key operational pillars include permissive hypotension (MAP ~50-65 mmHg) in non-head-injured patients pending surgical control, early balanced blood component transfusion ratios (1:1:1), and early tranexamic acid.

teaching_points.claim: Resuscitation must prioritize catastrophic external haemorrhage control first ('x-ABCDE') using commercial windlass tourniquets, wound packing with hemostatic gauze, and pelvic binders before managing airway or breathing.

Permissive hypotension (target systolic BP 80-90 mmHg, MAP 50-65 mmHg) is maintained in active bleeding without traumatic brain injury until definitive surgical or angiographic haemostasis is secured, preventing clot disruption and dilutional coagulopathy.

In polytrauma patients with concurrent severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), permissive hypotension is strictly contraindicated; systolic BP must be maintained >=100-110 mmHg to preserve cerebral perfusion pressure and prevent secondary brain necrosis.

Massive transfusion protocols (MTP) mandate early balanced blood product administration in a 1:1:1 ratio of packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets, which was shown in the PROPPR trial to significantly reduce death from exsanguination at 24 hours.

Hypothermia (core temperature <35 C) profoundly inhibits coagulation factor enzymatic activity and platelet function; active core warming, warmed blood products, and ambient resuscitation bay warming are mandatory.

uncertainties: Clinical superiority and logistics of pre-hospital and in-hospital low-titer group O positive or negative whole blood (LTO+WB) versus component therapy.
Indications and survival benefit of resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) versus emergency resuscitative thoracotomy in non-compressible torso hemorrhage.
mcq_angles: PROPPR trial findings: 1:1:1 ratio (plasma to platelets to RBCs) achieving faster hemostasis and lower 24-hour exsanguination mortality compared to 1:1:2.
Modifying permissive hypotension in the presence of severe traumatic brain injury (maintaining SBP >=100-110 mmHg).
Physiological impact of hypothermia and acidosis on coagulation enzyme kinetics: recognizing that factor activity drops by 10% for every 1 C drop in core temperature.
case_hooks: A 24-year-old male arrives in the trauma bay with a deep groin laceration from a chainsaw; the trauma leader immediately applies direct pressure and a junctional tourniquet ('x') before intubation.
A 35-year-old female with multiple gunshot wounds to the abdomen presents with BP 76/40 mmHg; the surgical team activates the MTP with balanced 1:1:1 components and infuses tranexamic acid 1 g.

page.mentor_intro: The coexistence of severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and systemic haemorrhagic shock represents a formidable clinical resuscitation dilemma. While damage control resuscitation for systemic trauma advocates permissive hypotension (systolic BP ~80-90 mmHg) to limit clot disruption, systemic hypotension in severe TBI doubles mortality by precipitating secondary cerebral ischemic injury. Resuscitation must aggressively prioritize cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) maintenance—strictly avoiding systolic BP <100-110 mmHg—alongside rapid haemostasis, normoxia, normocarbia, and timely surgical intracranial decompression.

teaching_points.claim: In patients with combined severe TBI and systemic haemorrhagic trauma, 'permissive hypotension' is strictly contraindicated; the Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines mandate maintaining systolic BP >=100 mmHg for patients aged 50-69 years and >=110 mmHg for patients aged 15-49 or >70 years to prevent secondary ischemic brain injury.
A single documented episode of systemic hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) or hypoxemia (PaO2 <60 mmHg / SpO2 <90%) in severe TBI is independently associated with a doubling of mortality.

Damage control fluid resuscitation in concomitant TBI requires balanced blood components (1:1:1 pRBC, FFP, platelets) or whole blood; hypotonic crystalloids (such as 0.9% normal saline with low osmolarity relative to injured brain, and especially Ringer's lactate with osmolarity ~273 mOsm/L) must be avoided to prevent worsening cerebral oedema.

Tranexamic acid (TXA) should be administered within 3 hours of injury in polytrauma patients with significant bleeding; in head injury (CRASH-3 trial), TXA reduces mortality in mild-to-moderate TBI without expanding intracranial hematomas.

uncertainties: Optimal blood pressure targets guided by non-invasive cerebral autoregulation monitoring (PRx) versus standardized SBP cutoffs in multi-trauma TBI.
Use of pre-hospital whole blood transfusion versus component therapy in polytrauma patients with blunt intracranial hemorrhage.
mcq_angles: Modifying permissive hypotension targets when severe traumatic brain injury coexists with torso haemorrhage (maintaining SBP >=100-110 mmHg).
Why hypotonic fluids (like Ringer's lactate) are avoided in severe TBI (hypotonicity increases brain tissue water content and elevates ICP).
Impact of secondary physiological insults (hypotension, hypoxia, hyperthermia, hypocapnia) on TBI mortality.
case_hooks: A 24-year-old unrestrained driver sustains blunt abdominal trauma with pelvic fracture and severe closed head injury (GCS 6); BP is 82/46 mmHg, and the trauma team must choose blood pressure targets and resuscitation fluids.
An intubated TBI patient in the trauma bay has a sudden drop in PaCO2 to 24 mmHg due to accidental hyperventilation on the transport ventilator, causing cerebral vasoconstriction.

page.mentor_intro: Intensive care management of severe traumatic brain injury (TBI, defined as post-resuscitation GCS <=8) focuses on the prevention, prompt detection, and aggressive mitigation of secondary brain injury. Secondary insults—ischemia, cellular energy failure, cerebral oedema, intracranial hypertension, and non-convulsive seizures—occur hours to days after the primary mechanical injury. A structured tier-based protocol coordinates mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic optimization targeting cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP 60-70 mmHg), automated pupillometry, temperature control, and multi-modality neuromonitoring.

teaching_points.claim: Continuous intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring is recommended in severe TBI patients (GCS <=8) with an abnormal admission head CT (hematomas, contusions, swelling, compressed basal cisterns) or normal CT with >=2 clinical risk factors (age >40, motor posturing, SBP <90 mmHg).

Guideline-directed management targets an ICP threshold <22 mmHg and a cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP) between 60 and 70 mmHg; avoiding CPP <60 mmHg prevents cerebral ischemia, while avoiding CPP >70 mmHg prevents hyperperfusion and ARDS.

Prophylactic post-traumatic seizure prevention with levetiracetam or phenytoin is recommended for the first 7 days following severe TBI to decrease early post-traumatic seizures; routine extension beyond 7 days is not recommended as it does not prevent late epilepsy.

Automated quantitative pupillometry (Neurological Pupil Index [NPI]) provides objective, operator-independent measurement of pupillary reactivity, detecting impending brain herniation and elevated ICP hours before gross clinical changes.

uncertainties: Utility of advanced multi-modality neuromonitoring (brain tissue oxygen tension [PbtO2] and microdialysis) in improving neurological recovery (BOOST-3 trial).
Optimal timing and patient selection for secondary decompressive craniectomy in medically refractory intracranial hypertension (RESCUEicp trial).
mcq_angles: Therapeutic target ranges for ICP (<22 mmHg) and CPP (60-70 mmHg) per Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines.
Duration and drug selection for post-traumatic seizure prophylaxis (7 days of levetiracetam or phenytoin; lack of benefit beyond 7 days).
Avoiding aggressive routine hyperventilation (PaCO2 <30-35 mmHg) due to profound cerebral vasoconstriction and secondary ischemic necrosis.
case_hooks: A 30-year-old male with severe TBI post-evacuation of an acute subdural hematoma has an external ventricular drain placed; monitor displays ICP 26 mmHg and MAP 82 mmHg (CPP = 56 mmHg).
A patient with severe TBI on day 3 in the neuro-ICU demonstrates a decline in automated pupillometry NPI from 4.2 to 2.1 in the left eye despite stable sedation.

page.mentor_intro: Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP >22 mmHg) following severe traumatic brain injury reflects the Monro-Kellie doctrine: within the rigid cranium, expanding volume (hematoma, brain oedema, vascular engorgement) compromises compensatory reserve, resulting in brain tissue herniation and death. Management utilizes a structured, tiered protocol escalating from basic neuroprotective foundations to advanced surgical and medical interventions. Tier 1 interventions include head elevation (30 degrees), midline neck positioning, analgesia/sedation, and CSF drainage; Tier 2 incorporates hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline); Tier 3 reserves decompressive craniectomy, barbiturate coma, or therapeutic hypothermia for refractory crises.

teaching_points.claim: Tier 1 baseline neuroprotective measures include: elevating the head of the bed to 30 degrees to optimize jugular venous outflow, maintaining the cervical spine in neutral midline position, ensuring normothermia (36-37 C), light-to-moderate sedation, and intermittent CSF drainage via external ventricular drain (EVD).

Tier 2 hyperosmolar therapy utilizes either equimolar boluses of mannitol (0.25 to 1.0 g/kg) or hypertonic saline (3% NaCl 150-250 mL bolus, or 23.4% NaCl 30 mL bolus); hypertonic saline is preferred in hemodynamically unstable or hypotensive patients as it expands plasma volume without inducing osmotic diuresis.

Mild hypocapnia (PaCO2 target 30-35 mmHg) may be utilized temporarily as a temporizing bridge for acute intracranial hypertension crises, but prolonged or severe hyperventilation (PaCO2 <30 mmHg) causes severe cerebral vasoconstriction and tissue ischemia.

Tier 3 therapies for refractory intracranial hypertension include surgical secondary decompressive craniectomy (RESCUEicp trial), high-dose continuous barbiturate infusion (pentobarbital or thiopental titrated to burst suppression), and deep neuromuscular blockade.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term neurological functional outcomes between 3% hypertonic saline continuous infusions versus intermittent bolus administration.
Safety and efficacy of ultra-early secondary decompressive craniectomy versus medical refractory rescue in diffuse brain swelling.
mcq_angles: Choosing between mannitol and hypertonic saline: why hypertonic saline is preferred in hypotensive trauma patients (preserves intravascular volume vs osmotic dehydration).
Understanding the dangers of prolonged hyperventilation in ICP management (cerebral vasoconstriction leading to brain tissue hypoxia).
Stepwise tier escalation for intracranial hypertension refractory to Tier 1 and Tier 2 measures.

page.mentor_intro: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis / Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) is a complex, chronic, multi-system neuroimmune disorder characterized by profound, incapacitating fatigue, cognitive impairment ('brain fog'), unrefreshing sleep, and orthostatic intolerance. Post-exertional malaise (PEM)—the pathognomonic hallmark of ME/CFS—is the dramatic worsening of multi-system symptoms following minor physical, cognitive, sensory, or emotional exertion that was previously tolerated. Crucially, symptoms typically flare 12 to 48 hours AFTER the exertion and can persist for days, weeks, or months; updated clinical guidelines (such as NICE NG206) explicitly reject graded exercise therapy (GET), establishing activity pacing as the foundational management strategy.

teaching_points.claim: Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is the defining clinical feature of ME/CFS, characterized by delayed (typically 12-48 hours post-exertion), disproportionate symptom exacerbation (fatigue, flu-like symptoms, pain, cognitive dysfunction) following minor physical or cognitive exertion.

Graded Exercise Therapy (GET)—which involves fixed, incremental increases in physical exercise—is explicitly contraindicated and rejected by international guidelines (e.g., NICE 2021 guidelines) because it triggers severe, prolonged PEM and causes clinical deterioration.

Pacing and energy envelope management is the primary evidence-based strategy for preventing PEM: patients identify their individual 'energy envelope', monitor heart rate (e.g., keeping heart rate below estimated anaerobic threshold, ~50-60% HRmax), and balance activity with proactive rest.

Orthostatic intolerance (POTS or neurally mediated hypotension) frequently exacerbates PEM in ME/CFS; management includes increased fluid and salt intake, compression garments, and pharmacologic therapy (fludrocortisone, midodrine, beta-blockers, or ivabradine).
Cognitive pacing (breaking intellectual tasks into short intervals with quiet rest) is as vital as physical pacing, as mental overexertion triggers identical neuroimmune and metabolic PEM flares.

uncertainties: Underlying cellular bioenergetic pathophysiology of PEM: role of mitochondrial electron transport chain impairment and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) uncoupling.
Clinical efficacy of low-dose naltrexone (LDN) and coenzyme Q10/NADH supplementation in mitigating neuroinflammation and reducing PEM severity.
mcq_angles: Pathognomonic feature of ME/CFS: delayed post-exertional malaise (PEM) occurring 12-48 hours after minor physical or cognitive exertion.
Contraindication of Graded Exercise Therapy (GET) per updated NICE and international guidelines.
Pacing mechanics: utilizing heart rate monitoring (staying below anaerobic threshold) to remain within the individual energy envelope.
case_hooks: A 34-year-old woman with ME/CFS following acute Epstein-Barr infection attempts a 20-minute brisk walk; 24 hours later she becomes bedbound with severe muscle aches, sore throat, and intense cognitive dysfunction lasting 5 days.

A physician reviews rehabilitation options for a patient with severe post-COVID-19 syndrome exhibiting PEM; the team explains why fixed-increment exercise programs must be avoided in favor of heart-rate-guided pacing.

page.mentor_intro: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a chronic, heterogeneous inflammatory spondyloarthritis affecting peripheral joints, axial spine, entheses (enthesitis), and digits (dactylitis), intimately associated with cutaneous psoriasis and nail dystrophy. Management follows domain-based treatment recommendations (GRAPPA and EULAR guidelines), selecting therapies according to active disease domains (peripheral arthritis, axial disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, skin, nails). Treatment escalates from NSAIDs and conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate) to targeted biological DMARDs—TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab), and IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab)—and targeted synthetic JAK inhibitors.

teaching_points.claim: Treatment selection in psoriatic arthritis is domain-driven: while conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine) are effective for peripheral arthritis, they are completely INEFFECTIVE for axial disease and enthesitis.

Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab) demonstrate robust efficacy across all clinical domains of PsA, including peripheral arthritis, axial disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, and radiographic structural progression.

Interleukin-17 (IL-17A and IL-17F) inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab) and IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab) provide superior cutaneous clearance (PASI 90/100) compared to TNF inhibitors, alongside equivalent peripheral articular efficacy.

In patients with prominent axial involvement or severe enthesitis refractory to NSAIDs, biologic therapy with a TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor should be initiated directly, bypassing ineffective conventional synthetic DMARDs.

uncertainties: Long-term disease-modifying potential of early biologic therapy in preventing the transition from cutaneous psoriasis to overt inflammatory psoriatic arthritis.
Comparative persistence and anti-drug antibody formation between fully humanized monoclonal antibodies and soluble receptor fusion proteins.
mcq_angles: Domain-specific efficacy: recognizing that methotrexate does not treat axial PsA or enthesitis.

Selecting IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitors over TNF inhibitors in patients with severe, extensive plaque psoriasis or concurrent inflammatory bowel disease considerations (IL-17 inhibitors are contraindicated in active Crohn disease).
Monitoring and safety screening before starting biologic DMARDs (latent tuberculosis screening, hepatitis B/C serology).

page.mentor_intro: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD)—defined clinically as the failure to achieve symptomatic remission despite adequate trials (dose and duration >=6-8 weeks) of at least two antidepressant medications from different pharmacological classes. TRD is associated with marked psychosocial impairment, increased healthcare utilization, and high suicide risk. When standard pharmacotherapies and oral augmentation (atypical antipsychotics, lithium) fail, advanced somatic and rapid-acting neuroplastic interventions are indicated: electroconvulsive therapy (ECT, the historical gold standard for efficacy) and glutamatergic modulators (intranasal esketamine and intravenous ketamine).

teaching_points.claim: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) remains the single most acutely effective intervention for severe treatment-resistant and psychotic depression, achieving response rates of 70-80% and rapid resolution of acute suicidal intent.

Right unilateral ultrabrief pulse ECT delivers clinical antidepressant efficacy comparable to bilateral ECT while dramatically reducing retrograde and anterograde cognitive and memory adverse effects.

Intravenous ketamine (0.5 mg/kg infused over 40 minutes) and intranasal esketamine (S-enantiomer, administered with oral antidepressant) produce rapid, robust antidepressant and anti-suicidal effects within 2 to 4 hours by blocking NMDA receptors and triggering AMPA-mediated BDNF synaptic neuroplasticity.

Maintenance strategies are mandatory following acute response to both ECT and ketamine/esketamine, as relapse rates exceed 50-60% within 1 to 3 months without continuation maintenance ECT (c-ECT) or ongoing scheduled esketamine dosing.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term cognitive outcomes and sustained durability between maintenance ECT and maintenance esketamine protocols in TRD.
Risk of dependency, bladder cystitis, and neurocognitive decline with repeated, multi-year ketamine infusions.
mcq_angles: Indications for urgent ECT: psychotic depression, severe catatonia, acute life-threatening suicidality, or severe malnutrition from depressive stupor.
Electrode placement and pulse width tradeoffs in ECT (bilateral vs right unilateral; ultrabrief pulse reducing cognitive/memory side effects).
Mechanism of action and administrative monitoring for intranasal esketamine (mandatory 2-hour clinical observation for sedation and blood pressure surges).
case_hooks: A 54-year-old woman with severe recurrent MDD fails sertraline, venlafaxine, and aripiprazole augmentation, presenting with profound depressive stupor and food refusal; urgent ECT is planned.

A 36-year-old male with severe TRD and active suicidal ideation receives an infusion of IV ketamine (0.5 mg/kg), experiencing substantial symptom relief and resolution of suicidal urges within 4 hours.

page.mentor_intro: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is etiologically divided into secondary (functional, >90% of cases) and primary (organic, <10%) valvular heart disease. Secondary TR is driven by annular dilation and leaflet tethering secondary to left-sided heart disease / pulmonary hypertension (ventricular functional TR) or atrial fibrillation with right atrial enlargement (atrial functional TR). Primary TR results from direct structural damage (endocarditis, carcinoid syndrome, rheumatic disease, congenital Ebstein anomaly, or pacemaker lead-induced leaflet perforation). Accurate differentiation dictates medical versus surgical or transcatheter intervention (TEER, transcatheter annuloplasty, heterotopic caval valve implantation, or transcatheter valve replacement).

teaching_points.claim: Functional (secondary) TR is characterized by normal tricuspid valve leaflet morphology with pathological annular dilation (>40 mm or >21 mm/m2) and leaflet tethering driven by RV pressure/volume overload or chronic atrial fibrillation (atrial functional TR).

Primary TR features intrinsic structural leaflet abnormalities—leaflet prolapse/flail, rheumatic retraction, carcinoid plaque thickening, infective endocarditis vegetations, or direct transvalvular pacemaker lead impingement/laceration.

Surgical tricuspid repair with a prosthetic annuloplasty ring is strongly indicated (Class I) at the time of left-sided valve surgery in patients with severe TR, or mild-to-moderate TR with significant annular dilatation (>=40 mm).

For isolated severe functional TR with high surgical risk, emerging transcatheter options include edge-to-edge repair (TEER: TriClip/PASCAL), transcatheter orthotopic valve replacement (TTVR: EVOQUE), and heterotopic caval valve implantation (CAVI: TricValve) for advanced non-reconstructible anatomy.

uncertainties: Optimal timing of intervention in asymptomatic severe functional TR to prevent irreversible right ventricular failure and cardiorenal syndrome.
Long-term thrombotic and durability outcomes of transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) in low-pressure right heart hemodynamics requiring anticoagulation.
mcq_angles: Differentiating atrial functional TR (isolated RA and annular dilation, preserved RV geometry) from ventricular functional TR (pulmonary hypertension, RV remodeling).
Indications for concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty during left-sided cardiac surgery based on annular dimension (diameter >=40 mm).
Role of heterotopic caval valve implantation (TricValve) in reducing systemic venous congestion when the tricuspid valve itself is untreatable.
case_hooks: A 72-year-old woman with long-standing permanent atrial fibrillation presents with massive tricuspid regurgitation, severe right atrial enlargement, tricuspid annular diameter 46 mm, but normal pulmonary artery pressures (atrial functional TR).

A 48-year-old male with a dual-chamber pacemaker implanted 3 years ago presents with new severe TR; echocardiography reveals the ventricular lead entangled and tethering the posterior tricuspid leaflet.

page.mentor_intro: Tricuspid transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) has emerged as a groundbreaking, minimally invasive percutaneous therapy for severe, symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation (TR) in patients at prohibitive or high surgical risk. Severe TR ('the forgotten valve disease') leads to progressive right ventricular dilation, hepatic congestion, peripheral oedema, and renal dysfunction, carrying high mortality with medical therapy alone. The landmark TRILUMINATE Pivotal trial demonstrated that T-TEER (using the TriClip device system) successfully reduces TR severity to moderate or less in >85% of patients, delivering significant, sustained improvements in health-related quality of life and functional capacity.

teaching_points.claim: The TRILUMINATE Pivotal trial established that tricuspid TEER safely and effectively reduces severe tricuspid regurgitation, achieving significant improvements in quality of life (KCCQ score) and functional status without excess procedural mortality.

Transoesophageal echocardiographic (TOE) procedural guidance—specifically simultaneous transgastric and multiplane mid-oesophageal views—is essential for accurate leaflet grasping across the anteroseptal and posteroseptal commissures.

Anatomical suitability criteria for T-TEER include: coaptation gap width (ideally <7 mm), sufficient leaflet length (>=8-10 mm), and absence of severe leaflet tethering or dense subvalvular pacemaker lead impingement.

Tricuspid regurgitation severity grading has expanded beyond traditional classifications to include 'massive' and 'torrential' grades (effective regurgitant orifice area [EROA] >=60-80 mm2), which still achieve substantial clinical benefit from grade reduction.

uncertainties: Long-term right ventricular reverse remodeling and survival benefit of transcatheter repair in patients with advanced pre-existing right ventricular systolic dysfunction (TAPSE <13 mm).
Comparative clinical efficacy and durability between tricuspid TEER and transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR: e.g., EVOQUE system).
mcq_angles: TRILUMINATE Pivotal trial outcomes: significant quality-of-life improvement with TriClip despite lacking a standalone 1-year mortality reduction.
Anatomical feasibility: identifying coaptation gap size (<7 mm) and leaflet mobility prerequisites for successful clip grasping.
Interference of transvenous cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) leads: assessing lead-induced vs lead-independent functional TR.
case_hooks: A 77-year-old woman with torrential functional tricuspid regurgitation, recurrent ascites, and multiple heart failure admissions despite high-dose loop diuretics is evaluated for percutaneous TriClip repair.
During T-TEER planning, intraprocedural transgastric short-axis TOE demonstrates a 4 mm coaptation defect between the anterior and septal tricuspid leaflets suitable for clip placement.

page.mentor_intro: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is an agonizing facial neuropathic pain disorder characterized by recurrent, sudden, unilateral, brief, electric shock-like paroxysmal pain restricted to one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (most commonly V2 and V3). Classical TN is caused by neurovascular conflict—neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root entry zone by an aberrant arterial loop (most commonly the superior cerebellar artery [SCA]), leading to focal demyelination and ephaptic transmission. Initial management relies on voltage-gated sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine as first-line gold standard), with early evaluation for microvascular decompression (MVD, Janetta procedure) in eligible patients with MRI-confirmed neurovascular compression.

teaching_points.claim: Carbamazepine (100-200 mg twice daily, titrated up to 800-1200 mg daily) and oxcarbazepine are the established first-line medical therapies for classical trigeminal neuralgia, providing initial pain relief in >80% of patients.

High-resolution 3D T2-weighted MRI (e.g., FIESTA or CISS sequences) coupled with 3D MR angiography is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice to visualize neurovascular conflict at the root entry zone and exclude secondary causes (multiple sclerosis plaques, cerebellopontine angle tumours).

Microvascular decompression (MVD) via retrosigmoid craniotomy is the most effective definitive surgical treatment for classical TN, achieving long-term pain freedom (>70-80% at 5-10 years) without sensory loss by dissecting the compressing vessel and placing an inert Teflon sponge prosthesis.

For elderly, frail patients or those without identifiable neurovascular conflict who fail medical therapy, percutaneous ablative rhizotomy procedures (radiofrequency thermocoagulation, balloon compression, glycerol rhizolysis) or stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife) provide effective less invasive alternatives, albeit with higher rates of facial numbness and recurrence.

uncertainties: Efficacy and safety of newer subtype-selective sodium channel blockers (e.g., Nav1.7 blockers) with fewer CNS and hyponatraemic side effects compared to carbamazepine.
Predictive value of artificial intelligence and automated radiomics in identifying truly symptomatic neurovascular compression on preoperative MRI.
mcq_angles: First-line pharmacotherapy for trigeminal neuralgia: carbamazepine optimization and monitoring (baseline CBC, liver function, and electrolytes for hyponatraemia).
Surgical mechanism and outcomes of microvascular decompression (MVD): identifying the superior cerebellar artery as the primary culprit vessel and placing a Teflon spacer.
Screening prerequisites: ruling out multiple sclerosis in young patients presenting with bilateral trigeminal neuralgia.

page.mentor_intro: Single-inhaler triple therapy (SITT)—combining an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS), a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA), and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) in a single device—represents an advanced maintenance therapy for chronic respiratory disease. In Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), landmark trials (IMPACT and ETHOS) established that triple therapy significantly reduces moderate-to-severe exacerbations and all-cause mortality compared to dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA) in patients with frequent exacerbations and elevated blood eosinophils (>=100-300 cells/uL). In severe uncontrolled asthma, adding a LAMA to ICS/LABA (CAPTAIN and TRIMARAN trials) significantly improves lung function and reduces exacerbations without requiring high-dose oral corticosteroids.

teaching_points.claim: In COPD, single-inhaler triple therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA, e.g., fluticasone furoate/umeclidinium/vilanterol or budesonide/glycopyrronium/formoterol) significantly reduces moderate-to-severe exacerbations and all-cause mortality compared to LAMA/LABA dual bronchodilation in patients with a history of exacerbations (IMPACT and ETHOS trials).

Blood eosinophil count serves as the primary predictive biomarker for ICS responsiveness in COPD: patients with blood eosinophils >=300 cells/uL (or >=100 cells/uL with >=2 moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalization) derive maximal exacerbation reduction and mortality benefit from adding ICS.

Inhaled corticosteroids in COPD increase the risk of bacterial pneumonia; patients with blood eosinophils <100 cells/uL, history of recurrent mycobacterial infections, or recurrent pneumonia derive negligible benefit from ICS and should be maintained on dual LAMA/LABA bronchodilators.

In persistent uncontrolled asthma, single-inhaler triple therapy provides significant improvements in FEV1 and reduces severe exacerbations across medium- and high-dose ICS formulations, serving as a critical step prior to or alongside biologic therapy.
Single-inhaler devices (SITT) improve patient adherence and reduce critical inhaler technique errors compared to multiple separate inhaler devices requiring different inhalation techniques.

uncertainties: Safety and criteria for step-down withdrawal of inhaled corticosteroids in stable COPD patients without frequent exacerbations maintained on dual bronchodilation (SUNSET trial).
Optimal positioning of single-inhaler triple therapy relative to targeted biologics (e.g., dupilumab) in severe eosinophilic COPD.
mcq_angles: IMPACT and ETHOS trial outcomes: all-cause mortality and exacerbation reduction with triple therapy over dual bronchodilation in symptomatic COPD.
Blood eosinophil thresholds: identifying which COPD patients benefit from ICS (>=300 cells/uL or >=100 with frequent exacerbations) vs those at risk for pneumonia without benefit (<100 cells/uL).
Single-inhaler versus multi-inhaler triple therapy: adherence advantages and eliminating conflicting peak inspiratory flow requirements.
case_hooks: A 64-year-old male with severe COPD on tiotropium/olodaterol sustains two severe hospital-treated exacerbations in the past year; blood eosinophil count is 380 cells/uL; he is transitioned to single-inhaler triple therapy.

A COPD patient with a blood eosinophil count of 40 cells/uL and a history of two episodes of severe bacterial pneumonia is reviewed; the pulmonologist de-escalates therapy from triple therapy to dual LAMA/LABA.

page.mentor_intro: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is defined immunohistochemically by the lack of oestrogen receptor (ER <1%), progesterone receptor (PR <1%), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) overexpression or gene amplification. Characterized by high histological grade, aggressive clinical trajectory, TP53 mutations, and propensity for visceral and central nervous system metastases, TNBC carries the poorest prognosis among breast cancer subtypes. Treatment paradigms integrate anthracycline/taxane-based chemotherapy, platinum salts, immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab), PARP inhibitors for germline BRCA carriers, and antibody-drug conjugates (sacituzumab govitecan) for advanced disease.

teaching_points.claim: Triple-negative breast cancer lacks ER, PR, and HER2 expression; all patients diagnosed with TNBC aged <=65 years (and all metastatic cases) must be referred for germline BRCA1/2 genetic testing.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with pembrolizumab significantly increases pathological complete response (pCR) rates and event-free survival in stage II-III early TNBC, with pembrolizumab continued postoperatively as adjuvant therapy (KEYNOTE-522 trial).

Pathological complete response (pCR, ypT0/is ypN0) after neoadjuvant therapy is a powerful surrogate for long-term overall survival; patients with residual invasive disease at surgical resection benefit from adjuvant capecitabine (CREATE-X trial) or olaparib if germline BRCA-mutated (OlympiA trial).

Sacituzumab govitecan—an antibody-drug conjugate targeting Trop-2 delivering the topoisomerase I inhibitor SN-38—delivers significant overall survival benefit in pretreated unresectable locally advanced or metastatic TNBC (ASCENT trial).

uncertainties: Necessity and duration of adjuvant pembrolizumab in patients who achieve complete pathological remission (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy.
Optimal sequencing between PARP inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates (sacituzumab govitecan, datopotamab deruxtecan) in metastatic BRCA-mutated TNBC.
mcq_angles: KEYNOTE-522 protocol: indications and duration of neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab in early high-risk TNBC.
Post-neoadjuvant adjuvant therapy in patients with residual invasive disease (capecitabine per CREATE-X vs olaparib for germline BRCA carriers per OlympiA).
Mechanism of action and indications for sacituzumab govitecan (Trop-2 ADC) in metastatic TNBC.
case_hooks: A 38-year-old woman presents with a rapidly growing 3.5 cm palpable breast mass and mobile axillary node; core biopsy reveals grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma, ER 0%, PR 0%, HER2 0, Ki-67 85%.

A 44-year-old female undergoes lumpectomy following neoadjuvant anthracycline/taxane/carboplatin therapy; surgical pathology reveals 1.2 cm residual invasive carcinoma (non-pCR) with negative margins.
