page.mentor_intro: Immunotherapy targeting the programmed cell death protein 1 / programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) axis has revolutionized the management of both early and advanced triple-negative breast cancer. Because TNBC possesses higher tumour mutational burden, greater stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), and higher PD-L1 expression compared to hormone receptor-positive subtypes, it is particularly susceptible to immune checkpoint blockade. In early TNBC, pembrolizumab is administered regardless of PD-L1 status (KEYNOTE-522), whereas in advanced/metastatic disease, pembrolizumab is restricted to tumours expressing PD-L1 with a Combined Positive Score (CPS) >=10 (KEYNOTE-355).

teaching_points.claim: In early-stage high-risk TNBC (T1c N1-2 or T2-4 N0-2), adding pembrolizumab to platinum/taxane/anthracycline neoadjuvant chemotherapy and continuing it adjuvantly for 9 cycles significantly increases pCR and reduces risk of distant recurrence or death (KEYNOTE-522).

In advanced or metastatic TNBC, pembrolizumab combined with first-line chemotherapy improves progression-free and overall survival ONLY in patients whose tumours express PD-L1 with a Combined Positive Score (CPS) >=10 (KEYNOTE-355 trial).

Immune-related adverse events (irAEs)—most commonly endocrinopathies (hypophysitis, primary hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency), dermatologic toxicities, and immune-mediated colitis/pneumonitis—require vigilant surveillance and prompt corticosteroid intervention.
Biomarkers of immune responsiveness in TNBC include stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (sTILs), high PD-L1 CPS, and high tumour mutational burden (TMB-H >=10 mut/Mb).

uncertainties: Predictive value of liquid biopsy circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) dynamics during neoadjuvant immunotherapy in identifying patients who can safely de-escalate adjuvant therapy.
Re-challenge safety and efficacy of checkpoint inhibitors in patients who previously discontinued immunotherapy due to Grade 2-3 irAEs.
mcq_angles: Contrasting PD-L1 biomarker requirements: neoadjuvant pembrolizumab in early TNBC is approved REGARDLESS of PD-L1, whereas metastatic first-line pembrolizumab REQUIRES CPS >=10.
Recognizing and managing adrenal insufficiency and hypophysitis in patients receiving checkpoint inhibitors presenting with vague fatigue, hyponatraemia, and hypotension.
Prognostic significance of stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (sTILs) in predicting spontaneous immune response and pCR.
case_hooks: A 49-year-old female with metastatic TNBC undergoes biopsy of a liver metastasis; immunohistochemistry reveals PD-L1 22C3 with a Combined Positive Score (CPS) of 18.
A patient receiving neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and paclitaxel presents with acute nausea, dizziness, BP 85/50 mmHg, and serum sodium 128 mmol/L; morning serum cortisol is 42 nmol/L.

page.mentor_intro: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS)—historically referred to as trochanteric bursitis—is a common regional pain syndrome characterized by tenderness over the greater trochanter of the femur and lateral hip. Modern imaging and surgical pathology demonstrate that true isolated bursitis is uncommon; rather, the primary pathology is gluteal tendinopathy or partial tearing of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus tendons (analogous to rotator cuff tears of the shoulder). Management emphasizes load management, progressive isometric-to-isotonic gluteal tendon strengthening, and avoiding passive stretching into adduction (which compresses the tendons against the trochanter).

teaching_points.claim: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) is primarily a gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy or insertional tear, rather than pure inflammation of the trochanteric bursa; histopathology shows non-inflammatory tendon degeneration.

Clinical diagnosis is established by localized point tenderness over the greater trochanter, reproducible lateral hip pain during single-leg stance for 30 seconds, resisted hip abduction, and the FADIR or FABER tests.

First-line management centers on mechanotherapy and load management: progressive isometric and isotonic hip abductor strengthening, pelvic control, and avoidance of sustained hip adduction (e.g., crossing legs, standing 'hanging on one hip', or sleeping on the affected side without a pillow between knees).

Local corticosteroid injections provide short-term symptomatic relief (up to 4-12 weeks) but do not confer long-term benefit over structured exercise therapy and carry small risks of tendon atrophy or rupture with repeated injections.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term clinical efficacy of leukocyte-rich platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections versus corticosteroid injections in chronic gluteal tendinopathy.
Surgical repair outcomes for high-grade gluteal tendon tears using open versus arthroscopic techniques.
mcq_angles: Differentiating GTPS from hip osteoarthritis: GTPS exhibits preserved passive hip internal/external rotation with localized lateral trochanteric palpation tenderness, whereas osteoarthritis causes groin pain and restricted internal rotation.
Mechanics of conservative exercise: avoiding tendon compression by eliminating passive adduction stretches (such as IT band stretches across midline).
Indications for MRI of the hip in recalcitrant GTPS (evaluating high-grade partial or full-thickness gluteus medius tears requiring surgical repair).
case_hooks: A 56-year-old woman presents with 6 months of aching lateral right hip pain that prevents her from sleeping on her right side; she has point tenderness over the greater trochanter and a positive 30-second single-leg stance test.
A patient with recalcitrant lateral hip pain refractory to two cortisone injections undergoes pelvic MRI, demonstrating a 1.5 cm full-thickness tear of the anterior gluteus medius tendon insertion.

page.mentor_intro: Tuberculosis (TB)—caused by the acid-fast bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis—is a chronic infectious granulomatous disease that primarily infects the lungs but can disseminate to any organ system. Transmission occurs via airborne droplet nuclei inhaled into pulmonary alveoli, where macrophages ingest bacilli, forming characteristic caseating granulomas (Ghon focus and complex). The clinical spectrum ranges from latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI, non-infectious, controlled by cell-mediated immunity) to active disease (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis); prompt molecular testing (GeneXpert MTB/RIF) and standardized multi-drug antimycobacterial therapy are mandatory.

teaching_points.claim: Active pulmonary TB diagnosis requires sputum rapid molecular testing with automated real-time PCR (GeneXpert MTB/RIF or Ultra), which detects M. tuberculosis DNA and simultaneous rifampicin resistance mutations (rpoB gene) within 2 hours.

Standard treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB consists of a 2-month intensive phase with four drugs—rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RHZE)—followed by a 4-month continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid (RH); pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is co-prescribed to prevent peripheral neuropathy.

Latent TB infection (LTBI) is diagnosed by tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs: QuantiFERON-TB Gold, T-SPOT.TB); short-course preventive regimens (3 months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid [3HP], or 4 months of daily rifampicin [4R]) are preferred over 9 months of isoniazid monotherapy.

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is the most common severe adverse effect of first-line therapy; pyrazinamide, isoniazid, and rifampicin are all hepatotoxic; therapy must be interrupted if serum transaminases exceed 5 times ULN (or >3 times ULN with jaundice or hepatitis symptoms).

Before initiating immunosuppressive biologic therapy (especially anti-TNF agents like infliximab or adalimumab), all patients must undergo mandatory screening for latent TB; active LTBI must be treated for at least 1 month before starting biologics to prevent fatal disseminated TB reactivation.

uncertainties: Efficacy and clinical safety of all-oral 6-month BPaL/BPaLM regimens in children and pregnant women with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
Host-directed adjunctive therapies (e.g., metformin, statins) to enhance macrophage autophagy and shorten antimycobacterial treatment duration.
mcq_angles: Action thresholds for drug-induced liver injury: stopping hepatotoxic TB medications when transaminases >5x ULN asymptomatic, or >3x ULN with symptoms.
Preferred short-course preventive regimens for latent TB: 3 months of once-weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid (3HP).
Mandatory latent TB screening before anti-TNF initiation: recognizing that TNF-alpha is essential for maintaining granuloma structural integrity.
case_hooks: A 28-year-old immigrant presents with 2 months of productive cough, drenching night sweats, and a 6 kg weight loss; chest radiograph reveals right upper lobe cavitary infiltrates; sputum GeneXpert is positive for MTB without rifampicin resistance.
A 45-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis is planned for infliximab; screening QuantiFERON-TB is positive with a normal chest radiograph; she begins 3HP preventive therapy.

page.mentor_intro: Tuberculosis: active vs latent TB, Mantoux, IGRA, NICE guidance, contact tracing is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

teaching_points.claim: Contemporary evidence synthesis highlights core pathophysiology, clinical staging, and multidisciplinary management: Undiagnosed burden of latent tuberculosis, active tuberculosis and tuberculosis-HIV co-infections in Africa-status quo, needs, priorities, and opportunities.

Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs: QuantiFERON-TB Gold, T-SPOT.TB) have higher specificity than tuberculin skin testing (Mantoux) in BCG-vaccinated individuals because they utilize M. tuberculosis-specific antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10).

Contact tracing for smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis requires household contact evaluation with symptom assessment, chest radiography, and IGRA testing to identify secondary transmission.

page.mentor_intro: Tuberculosis (TB) caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains one of the world's leading infectious causes of death. Standard treatment of drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis consists of a 6-month regimen divided into a 2-month intensive phase with four first-line bactericidal drugs—rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RHZE)—followed by a 4-month continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid (RH). Recent clinical breakthroughs have established shorter regimens: a 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen for drug-susceptible TB (Study 31), and 6-month all-oral regimens (BPaLM: bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) for multidrug-resistant/rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB).

teaching_points.claim: Standard first-line therapy for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB entails 2 months of daily RHZE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) followed by 4 months of daily RH (rifampicin, isoniazid); pyridoxine (vitamin B6, 25-50 mg daily) is co-administered to prevent isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.

The 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen (rifapentine, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and moxifloxacin for 2 months, followed by rifapentine, isoniazid, and moxifloxacin for 2 months) demonstrated non-inferiority to standard 6-month therapy in Study 31/A5349.

Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB, resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin) is now treated with the 6-month all-oral BPaLM regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid 600 mg, and moxifloxacin), which replaces historic 18-24 month toxic injectable-based regimens.

Baseline and on-treatment monitoring requires liver function testing (evaluating transaminitis from isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide; pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic), visual acuity and color discrimination (ethambutol optic neuritis), and complete blood count (linezolid myelosuppression).

uncertainties: Optimal linezolid dosing strategy (600 mg daily for 26 weeks vs 600 mg for 9-16 weeks followed by 300 mg) to minimize peripheral neuropathy and myelosuppression.
Role of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) for rifampicin and isoniazid in patients with diabetes mellitus, obesity, or HIV coinfection.
mcq_angles: Specific adverse effect profiles of first-line TB agents: ethambutol causing retrobulbar optic neuritis (red-green color blindness); pyrazinamide causing hyperuricaemia and hepatotoxicity; isoniazid causing neuropathy (prevented by vitamin B6).
Study 31 landmark 4-month regimen components (rifapentine + moxifloxacin + isoniazid + pyrazinamide).
All-oral 6-month BPaLM regimen for rifampicin-resistant/MDR-TB and monitoring linezolid haematologic toxicity.

page.mentor_intro: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous multi-system disorder caused by inactivating mutations in TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin), leading to constitutive hyperactivation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling cascade. Renal angiomyolipomas (AMLs)—benign triphasic mesenchymal tumours composed of dysplastic blood vessels, smooth muscle-like spindle cells, and mature adipose tissue—occur in up to 70-80% of TSC patients, typically presenting as bilateral, multifocal, and rapidly enlarging lesions. Unregulated aneurysmal vascular dilation confers high risk of life-threatening retroperitoneal haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome), requiring proactive surveillance and frontline mTOR inhibitor therapy (everolimus) or selective transcatheter arterial embolization.

teaching_points.claim: Renal angiomyolipomas in TSC carry a high risk of spontaneous retroperitoneal haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome), with risk correlating directly with tumour diameter >=4 cm or intralesional aneurysms >=5 mm.

Oral mTOR inhibitors (everolimus 10 mg daily) are the first-line pharmacologic treatment for growing or asymptomatic TSC-associated renal AMLs >=4 cm (EXIST-2 trial), achieving sustained tumour volume reduction of >=50% and preserving renal parenchyma.

For acute retroperitoneal haemorrhage or lesions refractory to/ineligible for mTOR inhibitors, selective transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) is the intervention of choice, minimizing normal nephron loss compared to surgical resection.

Total or radical nephrectomy is strictly contraindicated for TSC-associated angiomyolipomas except in cases of life-threatening uncontrollable haemorrhage or confirmed renal cell carcinoma, as multiple surgeries drive premature end-stage renal disease.

uncertainties: Rebound tumour regrowth rates following discontinuation of maintenance mTOR inhibitor therapy and long-term lowest effective maintenance dosing.
Distinguishing fat-poor renal angiomyolipoma from clear cell or chromophobe renal cell carcinoma on dual-energy CT and chemical shift MRI.
mcq_angles: Indications for initiating everolimus in TSC renal AML: asymptomatic growing AML >=4 cm to prevent retroperitoneal haemorrhage while preserving nephrons.
Management of acute rupture (Wunderlich syndrome): emergency selective transcatheter arterial embolization over nephrectomy.
Screening protocol: abdominal MRI every 1-3 years to monitor AML growth and intralesional microaneurysms.
case_hooks: A 26-year-old female with known tuberous sclerosis complex presents with sudden severe right flank pain and hypotension; emergency CT reveals a ruptured 6.5 cm right renal fat-containing mass with extensive retroperitoneal hematoma.

page.mentor_intro: Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is an oncologic emergency precipitated by massive, rapid lysis of malignant cells following initiation of cytotoxic therapy (or occasionally spontaneously in highly proliferative hematologic malignancies). Cellular breakdown releases immense quantities of potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids (catabolized into uric acid), overwhelming renal clearance and buffering mechanisms. The Cairo-Bishop definition distinguishes laboratory TLS (>=2 abnormalities: hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia) from clinical TLS (laboratory TLS plus acute kidney injury, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, or death); risk-stratified prophylaxis with aggressive hydration and hypouricaemic agents (allopurinol or rasburicase) is mandatory.

teaching_points.claim: Cairo-Bishop laboratory TLS requires >=2 of the following within 3-7 days of chemotherapy: uric acid >=476 umol/L (8 mg/dL), potassium >=6.0 mmol/L, phosphorus >=1.45 mmol/L (4.5 mg/dL), or corrected calcium <=1.75 mmol/L (7.0 mg/dL), or a 25% change from baseline.

Intravenous hydration (2-3 L/m2/day or 200 mL/m2/h targeting urine output >=100 mL/m2/h) is the cornerstone of TLS prophylaxis, maximizing glomerular filtration and flushing uric acid and calcium-phosphate crystals from renal tubules.

Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) prevents NEW uric acid formation and is indicated for intermediate-risk TLS; it does NOT degrade pre-existing uric acid and requires 24-48 hours to demonstrate full clinical effect.

Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) catalyzes the enzymatic conversion of uric acid into allantoin (5-10 times more soluble in urine), rapidly clearing pre-existing uric acid within 4 hours; it is indicated for high-risk TLS (Burkitt lymphoma, ALL with WBC >100,000, high-grade AML) or established hyperuricaemia.

Rasburicase is strictly contraindicated in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency due to severe risk of hydrogen peroxide-mediated acute haemolytic anaemia and methemoglobinaemia.

uncertainties: Cost-effectiveness and clinical non-inferiority of single fixed-dose rasburicase (e.g., 3 mg or 6 mg) versus weight-based daily dosing (0.2 mg/kg for 5 days).
Utility of urine alkalinization (routine bicarbonate infusion is no longer recommended as it promotes calcium phosphate precipitation in renal tubules).
mcq_angles: Differentiating allopurinol (blocks synthesis, for intermediate risk) from rasburicase (enzymatically degrades uric acid to allantoin, for high risk / existing hyperuricaemia).
Absolute contraindication to rasburicase: G6PD deficiency causing fatal acute hemolysis and methemoglobinaemia.
Laboratory sample handling for rasburicase: blood tubes must be kept on wet ice and analyzed immediately to avoid artifactual ex vivo uric acid degradation.

page.mentor_intro: Tumour Mutational Burden (TMB) and Microsatellite Instability-High (MSI-H) / Mismatch Repair Deficiency (dMMR) represent two pivotal, tissue-agnostic genomic biomarkers that predict exceptional clinical responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Defects in DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) lead to hypermutation, microsatellite length alterations, and generation of abundant immunogenic neoantigens that attract cytotoxic T-cell infiltration. Pembrolizumab achieved the first-ever histology-agnostic FDA approvals for MSI-H/dMMR solid tumours and high tumour mutational burden (TMB-H, defined as >=10 mutations per megabase [mut/Mb]), establishing comprehensive genomic profiling as an essential oncology tool.

teaching_points.claim: MSI-H / dMMR solid tumours generate high densities of frame-shift neoantigens, triggering intense tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte responses that are unleashed by anti-PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors, yielding durable response rates >40-50% across diverse cancer types.

Pembrolizumab carries landmark tissue-agnostic approvals for unresectable or metastatic MSI-H/dMMR solid tumours (KEYNOTE-158 trial) and for tumours with high tumour mutational burden (TMB-H >=10 mut/Mb, KEYNOTE-158).

In early-stage dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer, neoadjuvant dostarlimab (anti-PD-1 monotherapy for 6 months) achieved a remarkable 100% clinical complete response rate, eliminating the need for chemotherapy, radiation, or radical surgery in clinical trials.

Tumour mutational burden (TMB) is quantified via next-generation sequencing (NGS) comprehensive genomic profiling panels (e.g., FoundationOne CDx) measuring non-synonymous somatic mutations across coding regions.

All patients diagnosed with colorectal or endometrial cancer must undergo universal screening for dMMR via immunohistochemistry (loss of MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) or MSI PCR/NGS to screen for Lynch syndrome and guide immunotherapy.

uncertainties: Discrepancies in TMB cutoffs across different cancer histologies (whether 10 mut/Mb is equally predictive in non-melanoma/lung cancers compared to breast or prostate cancer).
Mechanism of primary resistance to PD-1 blockade occurring in ~20-30% of confirmed dMMR/MSI-H solid tumours.
mcq_angles: Tissue-agnostic threshold for TMB-H eligible for pembrolizumab: >=10 mutations/megabase (mut/Mb).
Universal screening indication for mismatch repair deficiency: all colorectal and endometrial carcinomas.
Paradigm-shifting neoadjuvant immunotherapy in dMMR rectal cancer: organ preservation with single-agent anti-PD-1 therapy.

A 42-year-old male with locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma is found to have complete loss of MSH2 and MSH6 on immunohistochemistry; genetic counselling evaluates for germline Lynch syndrome.

page.mentor_intro: Diabetes mellitus is a metabolic disorder characterized by chronic hyperglycaemia resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta-cells (islet autoantibodies: GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, anti-insulin), leading to absolute insulin deficiency and dependence on lifelong exogenous insulin replacement. Type 2 diabetes (T2D) arises from progressive insulin secretory defect superimposed on systemic insulin resistance, strongly associated with adiposity, metabolic syndrome, and polygenic risk; modern management focuses on cardiovascular and renal risk mitigation alongside glycaemic control.

teaching_points.claim: Type 1 diabetes requires mandatory lifelong insulin therapy (multiple daily injections [MDI] or automated insulin delivery [AID] hybrid closed-loop pump systems); continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is the standard of care to optimize time-in-range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL >70%) and prevent severe hypoglycaemia.

Screening for autoimmune T1D involves testing for circulating islet autoantibodies: glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65), insulinoma-associated protein 2 (IA-2), zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8), and islet cell antibodies (ICA).

In Type 2 diabetes with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), heart failure (HF), or chronic kidney disease (CKD), SGLT-2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) and/or GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, dulaglutide) are recommended independent of baseline HbA1c or metformin use.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) can occur in Type 2 diabetes as 'ketosis-prone diabetes' (Flatbush diabetes) and as 'euglycaemic DKA' (blood glucose <250 mg/dL) in patients taking SGLT-2 inhibitors, requiring urine or serum beta-hydroxybutyrate measurement.

uncertainties: Efficacy of disease-modifying anti-CD3 monoclonal antibodies (teplizumab) in delaying onset of clinical Stage 3 Type 1 diabetes in at-risk relatives.
Comparative long-term cognitive and microvascular benefits of dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists (tirzepatide) in early Type 2 diabetes.
mcq_angles: Differentiating late-onset autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA) from Type 2 diabetes: presence of GAD65 autoantibodies and rapid requirement for insulin within months to years.
Continuous glucose monitoring metrics: defining target Time in Range (TIR, 3.9-10.0 mmol/L [70-180 mg/dL]) >70% with Time Below Range (<3.9 mmol/L) <4%.
Recognizing euglycaemic DKA triggered by SGLT-2 inhibitors during acute illness, surgery, or low carbohydrate intake.

page.mentor_intro: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) results from autoimmune T-cell-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta-cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency. The landmark Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) and its long-term follow-up study (EDIC) established the foundation of modern diabetology: intensive insulin therapy significantly delays the onset and progression of diabetic microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular disease. This phenomenon—termed 'metabolic memory' or the legacy effect—demonstrates that early, stringent glycaemic control confers persistent vascular protection decades later.

teaching_points.claim: The DCCT trial demonstrated that intensive insulin therapy (target HbA1c <7.0% via multiple daily injections [MDI] or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion [CSII]) reduced diabetic retinopathy by 76%, nephropathy by 50%, and neuropathy by 60% compared to conventional therapy.

The long-term EDIC follow-up study proved the 'metabolic memory' phenomenon: patients in the original intensive treatment group continued to experience a 57% reduction in major cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death) decades later despite convergence of HbA1c levels.

Intensive glycemic control in the DCCT trial was accompanied by a 3-fold increase in severe hypoglycaemia; modern management utilizes continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and automated insulin delivery (AID / hybrid closed-loop systems) to achieve tight time-in-range (TIR >70%) while minimizing hypoglycaemia (time below range <4%).

Screening for microvascular complications should begin 5 years after diagnosis in type 1 diabetes (or at puberty), including annual dilated eye examinations, urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), and comprehensive foot sensory testing.

uncertainties: Cardiovascular and metabolic safety of adjunctive SGLT-2 or SGLT-1/2 inhibitors (e.g., sotagliflozin) in T1D, given the elevated risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis.
Long-term immunological preservation of residual C-peptide secretion using novel anti-CD3 monoclonal antibodies (teplizumab) in newly diagnosed Stage 3 T1D.
mcq_angles: DCCT trial landmark outcomes: intensive glycaemic control dramatically reduces microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy).
The concept of 'metabolic memory' (EDIC study): long-term cardiovascular protection stemming from early intensive control.
Standard CGM consensus targets for T1D: Time in Range (70-180 mg/dL [3.9-10.0 mmol/L]) >70%, and Time Below Range (<70 mg/dL [<3.9 mmol/L]) <4%.
case_hooks: A 22-year-old college student with type 1 diabetes on MDI has an HbA1c of 7.2% but experiences frequent nocturnal hypoglycaemia; transition to a hybrid closed-loop automated insulin delivery system reduces time below range from 9% to 1.5%.
A 35-year-old patient with a 15-year history of T1D undergoes annual screening; spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 85 mg/g, indicating microalbuminuria; an ACE inhibitor is initiated.

page.mentor_intro: Management of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus requires lifelong replacement of physiological insulin secretion, combining basal insulin (suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis overnight and between meals) and prandial bolus insulin (covering carbohydrate intake and correcting hyperglycaemia). The standard of care has transitioned from fingerstick glucose testing and static dosing to digital diabetes technology: continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) integrated with automated insulin delivery (AID) hybrid closed-loop systems. Comprehensive management mandates structured carbohydrate counting, exercise management, sick-day rules, blood ketone monitoring to prevent diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), and screening for associated autoimmune conditions (celiac disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis).

teaching_points.claim: Physiological basal-bolus insulin regimens utilize long-acting basal analogues (degludec, glargine U-300) combined with rapid-acting prandial analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) or ultra-rapid formulations, matching doses to carbohydrate intake using insulin-to-carbohydrate ratios (ICR) and correction factors (insulin sensitivity factor [ISF]).

Automated Insulin Delivery (AID / hybrid closed-loop) systems modulate basal insulin delivery in real-time based on continuous sensor glucose trends, significantly increasing Time in Range (TIR) and reducing nocturnal hypoglycaemia compared to sensor-augmented pumps or multiple daily injections.

Sick-day rules are vital to prevent DKA during acute intercurrent illness: patients must NEVER stop insulin (even if fasting or vomiting), check blood glucose every 2-4 hours, monitor blood beta-hydroxybutyrate levels, hydrate with oral fluids, and administer supplemental rapid-acting correction insulin.

All patients diagnosed with type 1 diabetes must undergo baseline and periodic screening for concurrent autoimmune diseases: thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies/TSH for autoimmune thyroid disease, and tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) for celiac disease.

Severe hypoglycaemia management requires prescription of emergency glucagon (intranasal dry powder glucagon 3 mg [Baqsimi] or ready-to-use subcutaneous auto-injectors) provided to all family members and caregivers.

uncertainties: Optimal exercise algorithms for hybrid closed-loop AID systems during high-intensity interval training (HIIT, which causes catecholamine-mediated hyperglycaemia) versus prolonged aerobic exercise.
Role of stem cell-derived allogeneic or autologous islet cell transplantation without chronic immunosuppression (e.g., encapsulated or gene-edited islets).
mcq_angles: Sick-day management: why basal insulin must never be discontinued during acute illness even when oral intake is reduced.
Emergency treatment of severe hypoglycaemia outside hospital: non-invasive intranasal glucagon (3 mg single dose).
Screening for concurrent autoimmune diseases in T1D: universal screening for celiac disease (tTG-IgA) and thyroiditis (TSH/anti-TPO).
case_hooks: A 19-year-old female with T1D develops gastroenteritis with vomiting; assuming she does not need insulin because she cannot eat, she omits her basal insulin and arrives 16 hours later in severe DKA (pH 7.10, ketones 5.8 mmol/L).

A 26-year-old male with T1D has persistent bloating and iron-deficiency anaemia despite good glycaemic control; screening tTG-IgA is elevated at 120 U/mL, and duodenal biopsy confirms celiac enteropathy.

page.mentor_intro: Cardiovascular disease is the principal cause of morbidity and premature mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D). A paradigm shift in diabetology has transformed management from glucose-centric glucocentric targets to organ-protective cardiorenal medicine. Cardiovascular outcomes trials (CVOTs) have definitively demonstrated that sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) confer dramatic, independent reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), heart failure hospitalizations, and progressive diabetic kidney disease.

teaching_points.claim: SGLT-2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) reduce hospitalization for heart failure by 30-35% and attenuate renal disease progression across the entire ejection fraction spectrum in patients with and without diabetes (EMPA-REG OUTCOME, DAPA-HF, DELIVER).

GLP-1 receptor agonists with proven cardiovascular benefit (subcutaneous semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) significantly reduce 3-point MACE (cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) by 12-14% in T2D patients with established ASCVD or high cardiovascular risk (LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, REWIND).
The FLOW trial demonstrated that semaglutide 1.0 mg weekly reduces the risk of major kidney disease events and cardiovascular death by 24% in patients with T2D and chronic kidney disease.

Current international guidelines mandate co-prescribing SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs for T2D patients with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or CKD, irrespective of whether the baseline HbA1c is already at target.

uncertainties: Additive cardiovascular benefit and tolerability of combining SGLT-2 inhibitors with dual GLP-1/GIP agonists (tirzepatide) in high-risk ASCVD cohorts.
Cardiovascular safety and long-term MACE reduction of non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (finerenone) when added on top of combined SGLT-2 inhibitor and GLP-1 RA therapy.
mcq_angles: Matching drug class to primary cardiovascular phenotype: SGLT-2 inhibitors are the preferred class for heart failure and CKD progression; GLP-1 RAs are preferred for ASCVD/stroke reduction and weight reduction.
EMPA-REG OUTCOME and DAPA-HF landmark findings: early divergence of heart failure and mortality curves with SGLT-2 inhibition.
Indications for GLP-1 RA in chronic kidney disease based on the landmark FLOW trial.
case_hooks: A 62-year-old male with T2D and an anterior STEMI 2 years ago has HbA1c 6.8% on metformin; the cardiologist discusses adding empagliflozin and semaglutide despite excellent glycaemic control.
A 67-year-old woman with T2D and diabetic nephropathy (eGFR 38 mL/min, UACR 450 mg/g) is evaluated for renal-protective pharmacotherapy.

page.mentor_intro: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) is a progressive cardiometabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell dysfunction. Modern management has shifted from a purely glucocentric paradigm (lowering HbA1c alone) to an organ-protective cardiorenal approach. In patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), heart failure (HF), or chronic kidney disease (CKD), guideline-directed medical therapy prioritizes sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) independent of baseline HbA1c or metformin use.

teaching_points.claim: Metformin remains the foundational first-line oral agent for glycaemic control when organ-specific indications do not dictate otherwise, provided estimated GFR is >=30 mL/min/1.73m2 (holding or reducing dose by 50% if eGFR 30-44 mL/min to prevent lactic acidosis).

In patients with T2D and established ASCVD or high cardiovascular risk, a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) is recommended to reduce 3-point MACE (myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death).

In patients with T2D and heart failure (HFrEF or HFpEF) or chronic kidney disease (eGFR 20-60 mL/min or UACR >30 mg/g), SGLT-2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) are strongly recommended to reduce heart failure hospitalizations and renal progression.

Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists (tirzepatide) deliver unprecedented reductions in HbA1c (>2.0-2.5%) and substantial weight loss (>15-20%), representing the most potent glucose- and weight-lowering agent in the SURPASS clinical trial program.

Glycaemic targets must be individualized: HbA1c <7.0% (<53 mmol/mol) for most non-pregnant adults without severe hypoglycaemia, while relaxed targets (HbA1c <7.5-8.0%) are appropriate for frail older adults with limited life expectancy or extensive vascular complications.

uncertainties: Additive long-term cardiovascular and microvascular outcomes of combining dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists (tirzepatide) with SGLT-2 inhibitors.
Durable diabetes remission criteria following intensive lifestyle intervention versus metabolic bariatric surgery in early-stage T2D.
mcq_angles: Selecting second-line therapy based on compelling comorbidities: SGLT-2 inhibitor for heart failure/CKD vs GLP-1 RA for ASCVD/weight loss.
Metformin renal safety thresholds: dose reduction at eGFR <45 mL/min, and absolute contraindication/discontinuation at eGFR <30 mL/min.
SGLT-2 inhibitor adverse effects: mycotic genital infections, volume depletion, and recognizing euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA).
case_hooks: A 58-year-old male with T2D, prior CABG, and eGFR 48 mL/min has HbA1c 7.6% on metformin; the clinician adds empagliflozin to provide cardiorenal protection.
A 52-year-old woman with severe obesity (BMI 38 kg/m2) and uncontrolled T2D (HbA1c 9.4%) is initiated on weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide with rapid glycaemic and weight improvement.

page.mentor_intro: The management of type 2 diabetes mellitus combines holistic lifestyle intervention with organ-protective pharmacotherapy tailored to patient-specific cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic risk profiles. Modern glycemic targets emphasize individualized HbA1c goals while avoiding hypoglycemia.

teaching_points.claim: Type 2 diabetes pathogenesis combines progressive pancreatic beta-cell secretory dysfunction with peripheral insulin resistance in skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue; modern glycemic management prioritizes organ-protective agents (SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists) independent of baseline HbA1c in patients with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease.

Glycemic targets are individualized: standard target HbA1c is <=7.0% (53 mmol/mol) for most non-pregnant adults to prevent microvascular complications, tighter targets (<6.5%) for young patients without cardiovascular disease, and relaxed targets (7.5-8.5%) for frail older adults with limited life expectancy or severe hypoglycemia risk.

Metformin remains the foundational first-line oral antihyperglycemic agent, acting primarily by inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMPK activation; it requires dose adjustment when eGFR is 30-45 mL/min/1.73m2 and is contraindicated when eGFR is <30 mL/min/1.73m2 due to lactic acidosis risk.

SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) reduce cardiovascular death, heart failure hospitalizations, and CKD progression, while GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, dulaglutide) demonstrate robust reductions in atherosclerotic cardiovascular events (MACE) and provide substantial weight reduction.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing of dual SGLT2 inhibitor and GLP-1 receptor agonist combination therapy in early diabetic kidney disease.
Durability of non-insulin glycemic control using dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor co-agonists (tirzepatide) in advanced beta-cell failure.
mcq_angles: First-line agent selection based on comorbidities: SGLT2 inhibitors preferred in HFrEF/HFpEF and CKD; GLP-1 RAs preferred in established ASCVD and severe obesity.
Metformin renal cutoffs: safe down to eGFR 45; maximum 1000 mg daily for eGFR 30-45; stop when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m2.
Hypoglycemia risk profiles: sulfonylureas and insulins carry high hypoglycemia risk; metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, and GLP-1 RAs carry negligible intrinsic hypoglycemia risk.

Enteric (typhoid) fever caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi presents with step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), rose spots, and hepatosplenomegaly; blood culture is the definitive diagnostic gold standard (Widal test is unreliable due to high false-positive and false-negative rates); empirical first-line treatment for travelers returning from endemic areas (South Asia) is intravenous ceftriaxone or high-dose oral azithromycin due to widespread fluoroquinolone resistance.

page.mentor_intro: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic idiopathic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by diffuse, continuous mucosal inflammation commencing in the rectum and extending proximally to variable extents of the colon. Disease extent is classified by the Montreal classification into proctitis (E1), left-sided colitis (E2), and extensive/pancolitis (E3), presenting clinically with bloody diarrhoea, rectal urgency, tenesmus, and cramping abdominal pain. Management follows a 'treat-to-target' strategy (STRIDE-II), aiming not merely for symptomatic relief but for objective endoscopic mucosal healing (Mayo endoscopic subscore 0 or 1) and histologic remission to prevent dysplasia, colectomy, and colorectal cancer.

teaching_points.claim: 5-Aminosalicylates (5-ASA, mesalazine) are the first-line therapy for inducing and maintaining remission in mild-to-moderate UC; combined oral plus topical rectal 5-ASA therapy is significantly superior to oral mesalazine monotherapy for left-sided and extensive colitis.

Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or IV hydrocortisone) are highly effective for inducing remission in moderate-to-severe acute flares, but have NO role in maintenance therapy due to lack of mucosal healing and severe steroid-related toxicities.

Acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC)—defined by Truelove and Witts criteria (>=6 bloody stools/day plus >=1 systemic sign: pulse >90, temp >37.8 C, Hb <105 g/L, or ESR >30 mm/h)—is a medical emergency requiring hospitalization, IV methylprednisolone, and objective day 3 response assessment (Oxford criteria) to trigger rescue therapy (infliximab or cyclosporine).

Long-term surveillance colonoscopy with dye-spray chromoendoscopy is mandatory starting 8 years after symptom onset in patients with left-sided or extensive colitis, repeated every 1 to 5 years based on risk factors (primary sclerosing cholangitis, active inflammation, family history of CRC).

Restorative proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA, 'J-pouch') is the surgical procedure of choice for medically refractory ulcerative colitis, acute toxic megacolon, or colonic high-grade dysplasia/adenocarcinoma.

uncertainties: Comparative safety and clinical positioning of oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) versus anti-IL-23 antibodies (mirikizumab, guselkumab) in moderate-to-severe UC.
Role of faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) as an adjunctive induction therapy in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis.
mcq_angles: First-line induction and maintenance in mild-to-moderate UC: superior efficacy of combined oral plus rectal 5-ASA over oral alone.
Truelove and Witts criteria for acute severe UC (ASUC) and day 3 Oxford criteria triggering rescue therapy with infliximab or cyclosporine.
Dysplasia surveillance timing: initiating screening colonoscopy at 8 years post-diagnosis in extensive or left-sided colitis (annual in primary sclerosing cholangitis).
case_hooks: A 26-year-old female presents with 8 bloody bowel movements per day, resting heart rate 104 bpm, temperature 38.1 C, and CRP 48 mg/L (Truelove and Witts acute severe UC); she is admitted for IV corticosteroids.
A 34-year-old male with left-sided ulcerative colitis has persistent rectal bleeding on oral mesalazine 4 g daily; adding a nightly 1 g mesalazine suppository induces complete symptomatic remission.

page.mentor_intro: Advanced therapies for moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis encompass diverse mechanistic classes: TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab), gut-selective anti-integrin alpha4beta7 (vedolizumab), anti-IL-12/23 (ustekinumab), anti-IL-23 p19 inhibitors (mirikizumab, guselkumab), oral JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib), and sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulators (ozanimod, etrasimod). Network meta-analyses and head-to-head randomized trials (e.g., the landmark VARSITY trial) provide high-quality evidence guiding personalized drug selection based on speed of onset, endoscopic remission rates, prior biologic exposure, and patient safety profiles.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark VARSITY trial—the first direct head-to-head randomized trial of biologics in moderate-to-severe UC—demonstrated that gut-selective vedolizumab was significantly superior to the anti-TNF agent adalimumab in achieving clinical remission (31.3% vs 22.5%, p = 0.006) and endoscopic mucosal healing at week 52.

In biologic-naive patients, infliximab and vedolizumab rank among the highest for induction and maintenance of clinical and endoscopic remission; infliximab is co-prescribed with an immunomodulator (thiopurine) to reduce anti-drug antibody formation and loss of response.

Upadacitinib (oral selective JAK-1 inhibitor) demonstrates the highest rates of rapid clinical response and endoscopic mucosal healing among oral agents in network meta-analyses, functioning as an exceptionally potent option for both biologic-naive and biologic-experienced refractory patients.

Vedolizumab and ustekinumab exhibit the most favorable overall infection and malignancy safety profiles, making them preferred first-line advanced therapies in elderly patients (>60-65 years) or those with prior opportunistic infections.

Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulators (ozanimod, etrasimod) provide oral advanced therapy options by sequestering lymphocytes in lymph nodes; pre-treatment screening requires ECG (evaluating bradyarrhythmias/AV block), ophthalmic exam (excluding macular edema), and varicella zoster immunity.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term effectiveness of novel IL-23 p19-specific inhibitors (mirikizumab, guselkumab) versus JAK inhibitors in multi-biologic refractory ulcerative colitis.
Safety and efficacy of dual targeted therapy (e.g., combining vedolizumab with a JAK inhibitor or anti-TNF) in highly refractory IBD.
mcq_angles: VARSITY trial landmark findings: vedolizumab demonstrated superior clinical remission and endoscopic mucosal improvement over adalimumab in moderate-to-severe UC.
Safety stratification in elderly patients with UC: selecting gut-selective vedolizumab or ustekinumab over anti-TNF or JAK inhibitors due to lower infection/thromboembolism risk.
Pre-treatment screening requirements for S1P receptor modulators (ozanimod): baseline ECG for conduction block, macular edema screening, and VZV serology.
case_hooks: A 68-year-old male with moderate-to-severe UC and a history of myocardial infarction and diverticulitis requires advanced therapy; the gastroenterologist selects vedolizumab due to its gut-selective safety profile.

page.mentor_intro: Upper Airway Resistance Syndrome (UARS) is a sleep-disordered breathing condition positioned along the spectrum between simple snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). UARS is characterized by repetitive increases in upper airway resistance during sleep that do not meet classic criteria for apnoeas or hypopneas, but produce increased respiratory effort leading to micro-arousals (Respiratory Effort-Related Arousals [RERAs]) and sleep fragmentation. Patients typically present with excessive daytime sleepiness, chronic fatigue, morning headaches, and insomnia, frequently without prominent obesity or severe oxygen desaturation, and are commonly misdiagnosed with fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, or depression.

teaching_points.claim: UARS is characterized by repetitive Respiratory Effort-Related Arousals (RERAs) without significant hypoxemia; polysomnography demonstrates an Apnoea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) <5 events/hour, but an elevated Respiratory Disturbance Index (RDI >=5-15 events/hour, where RDI = AHI + RERA index).

Pathophysiology involves dynamic inspiratory flow limitation (flattening of the inspiratory nasal cannula pressure transducer wave) caused by subtle structural narrowing of the pharynx, nasal cavity, or retroglottic space.

Unlike typical OSA patients who are frequently obese males, UARS patients are commonly young, lean females with anatomical craniofacial variations (narrow retrognathic mandible, high-arched hard palate, nasal septal deviation, inferior turbinate hypertrophy).

First-line treatment is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), which eliminates inspiratory flow limitation and normalizes sleep architecture; alternative therapies include customized mandibular advancement devices (MAD) and targeted otorhinolaryngologic surgery (septoplasty, turbinoplasty).

uncertainties: Diagnostic reliability and standardization of automated scoring algorithms for RERAs across different sleep laboratory software systems.
Long-term cardiovascular sequelae and hypertension risk in untreated UARS compared to obstructive sleep apnoea.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic definition of UARS on polysomnography: AHI <5 events/hour with elevated RDI (RERAs causing cortical arousals) in the absence of severe oxygen desaturation.
Recognizing the clinical phenotype: lean individuals, daytime fatigue, insomnia, functional somatic symptoms, and subtle craniofacial crowding.
Waveform hallmark on polysomnography: flattened inspiratory contour on nasal pressure cannula tracing reflecting flow limitation.

page.mentor_intro: Acute gastrointestinal bleeding is a critical clinical presentation bifurcated by the ligament of Treitz into upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) and lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB). UGIB commonly arises from peptic ulcer disease, gastroduodenal erosions, Mallory-Weiss tears, and oesophageal/gastric varices, manifesting as haematemesis or melaena with an elevated blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratio (>20-30:1). LGIB originates distal to the ligament of Treitz (diverticular bleeding, angiodysplasia, ischemic colitis, haemorrhoids, neoplasms), typically presenting as haematochezia; initial management across both mandates rapid hemodynamic stabilization, risk stratification (Glasgow-Blatchford and Oakland scores), and timely endoscopy.

teaching_points.claim: Initial management for both UGIB and LGIB prioritizes airway, breathing, and circulation: establishing two large-bore peripheral IV lines (16G or 18G), fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloids, and restrictive transfusion targeting haemoglobin 70-80 g/L (7-8 g/dL) in stable patients without acute coronary syndrome.

The Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) is the superior validated risk tool for acute UGIB; a score of 0-1 identifies very low-risk patients who can safely be discharged without inpatient admission, while scores >=6 predict high risk of rebleeding and intervention.

For acute non-variceal UGIB, intravenous proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy (e.g., omeprazole 80 mg IV bolus followed by 8 mg/h infusion, or 40 mg IV twice daily) stabilizes gastric pH >6 to promote platelet aggregation and clot formation prior to endoscopy.

In patients presenting with massive haematochezia and hemodynamic shock, an upper GI bleed must always be excluded (brisk duodenal bleeding with rapid transit), warranting immediate upper endoscopy prior to colonoscopy.
For acute LGIB, the Oakland score predicts safe outpatient discharge (score <=8); colonoscopy is performed after complete oral purgative bowel preparation in hospitalized patients.

uncertainties: Optimal timing of colonoscopy in acute lower GI bleeding (urgent <24 hours versus elective after elective bowel prep during admission).
Optimal timing for restarting therapeutic anticoagulation and antiplatelet agents following endoscopically verified haemostasis.
mcq_angles: Distinguishing massive UGIB from LGIB: recognizing that rapid upper GI bleeding can present with bright red haematochezia and a markedly elevated BUN/creatinine ratio (>20-30).
Applying the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS): identifying low-risk scores (0-1) eligible for outpatient management.
Restrictive red blood cell transfusion threshold (70-80 g/L) versus liberal transfusion (100 g/L) in acute GI bleeding, reducing rebleeding and mortality.
case_hooks: A 68-year-old man taking naproxen presents with melaena, BP 92/58 mmHg, HR 118 bpm, Hb 74 g/L, and BUN 18.2 mmol/L with creatinine 85 umol/L; GBS is 12, prompting emergency resuscitation and endoscopy.
A 74-year-old woman presents with painless bright red blood per rectum and stable vital signs; the clinical team calculates an Oakland score of 7 and plans outpatient colonoscopic workup.

page.mentor_intro: Management of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) coordinates emergency hemodynamic resuscitation, risk stratification, empiric medical therapies, and therapeutic upper endoscopy within 24 hours. Endoscopic evaluation establishes etiology—most frequently peptic ulcer disease (PUD, ~50%), followed by oesophagogastric varices, erosive gastritis, and Mallory-Weiss tears. For peptic ulcers, the Forrest classification determines endoscopic haemostasis (high-risk stigmata: Forrest Ia spurting, Ib oozing, IIa non-bleeding visible vessel, and IIb adherent clot), utilizing dual multimodal endoscopic techniques (epinephrine injection combined with thermal coagulation, mechanical hemoclips, or hemostatic powders).

teaching_points.claim: Early risk stratification using the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) should be performed upon presentation; endoscopy should be performed within 24 hours of presentation after initial hemodynamic resuscitation (ultra-early endoscopy <6 hours does not improve clinical outcomes in non-variceal bleeding).

High-risk peptic ulcer lesions (Forrest Ia, Ib, and IIa) mandate dual-modality endoscopic haemostasis (e.g., hemoclip or bipolar electrocoagulation PLUS dilute epinephrine injection), followed by high-dose intravenous PPI therapy for 72 hours.

Pre-endoscopic administration of a single intravenous dose of erythromycin (250 mg IV 30-60 minutes prior) promotes gastric emptying of blood and clots, significantly improving endoscopic visualization and reducing the need for repeat procedures.

Testing for Helicobacter pylori is mandatory in all patients with bleeding peptic ulcers; initial biopsy during acute bleeding carries high false-negative rates, requiring confirmation with stool antigen or urea breath test 4-6 weeks post-bleed off PPIs.
Transfusion strategy should be restrictive (transfusion trigger Hb <70 g/L, target 70-90 g/L), except in patients with active acute coronary syndromes (target Hb >=80-100 g/L) (Villanueva trial).

uncertainties: Efficacy of topically applied hemostatic powders (e.g., Hemospray, TC-325) as primary standalone therapy versus rescue therapy for refractory non-variceal bleeding.
Safety and timing of early oral feeding in patients following successful endoscopic treatment of high-risk ulcers.
mcq_angles: Forrest classification and endoscopic intervention thresholds: identifying which lesions require active treatment (Ia, Ib, IIa, and selected IIb) versus clean-based ulcers (III) which do not.
Role of pre-procedure IV erythromycin in clearing the gastric fundus and improving mucosal visualization.

Managing recurrent ulcer bleeding following initial successful endoscopy: repeat endoscopic intervention is preferred first-line over immediate emergency surgery or transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE).
case_hooks: A 55-year-old male presents with haematemesis; endoscopy reveals a 1.5 cm duodenal bulb ulcer with a pigmented non-bleeding visible vessel (Forrest IIa); dual-modality haemostasis with hemoclips and thermal probe is performed.

A 70-year-old female with a bleeding gastric ulcer tests negative for H. pylori on rapid urease biopsy performed during active haemorrhage; the physician arranges confirmatory testing after discharge.

page.mentor_intro: An acute upper GI bleed (UGIB) presents classically with haematemesis (bright red blood or 'coffee-ground' emesis) and/or melaena (black, tarry, foul-smelling stool resulting from the oxidation of heme by intestinal bacteria). In patients presenting with severe, brisk hematochezia accompanied by hemodynamic instability or shock, an upper source must always be considered due to rapid transit of massive blood loss through the GI tract. Core management pillars include securing the airway in actively vomiting or encephalopathic patients, hemodynamic resuscitation, pre-endoscopic prokinetic administration (erythromycin), and multimodal endoscopic haemostasis.

teaching_points.claim: Rapid gastrointestinal transit of massive upper GI bleeding (>1000 mL) can present with bright red hematochezia and hemodynamic shock; an elevated blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratio (>20-30:1 in conventional units, or >100 in SI units) strongly supports an upper GI source.

Elective endotracheal intubation should be considered prior to upper endoscopy in patients with active hematemesis, severe altered mental status (hepatic encephalopathy), or ongoing agitation to prevent catastrophic pulmonary aspiration.

Pre-procedure intravenous erythromycin (250 mg IV infused 30-60 minutes prior to endoscopy) acts as a motilin agonist to clear blood, clots, and debris from the stomach, significantly improving endoscopic mucosal visualization and diagnostic yield.

For non-variceal peptic ulcers with high-risk stigmata (Forrest Ia spurting, Ib oozing, IIa non-bleeding visible vessel), dual endoscopic therapy (epinephrine injection PLUS mechanical hemoclips or thermal contact probe) is mandatory; epinephrine monotherapy is strictly inadequate due to high rebleeding rates.

Endoscopic band ligation (EVL) is the gold standard for esophageal variceal bleeding; in fundic gastric varices (GOV2/IGV1), endoscopic tissue adhesives (cyanoacrylate glue injection) or transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is required.

uncertainties: Role of over-the-scope clips (OTSC) as first-line therapy versus conventional through-the-scope clips (TTSC) for large (>2 cm) fibrotic chronic peptic ulcers.
Efficacy and clinical safety of topical hemostatic powders (e.g., Hemospray) as temporary bridge therapy in massive malignant upper GI bleeding.
mcq_angles: BUN/creatinine ratio utility: elevated ratio (>20-30:1) distinguishing brisk upper GI bleed from lower GI hemorrhage in hematochezia.
Dual-modality endoscopic haemostasis requirement for high-risk peptic ulcers: mechanical or thermal therapy combined with epinephrine.
Endoscopic management of gastric fundic varices: cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive injection rather than band ligation.
case_hooks: A 52-year-old male presents with massive hematochezia and syncope; BP is 80/50 mmHg; nasogastric lavage yields bright red blood with clots, confirming an upper gastrointestinal origin.

During emergency gastroscopy for bleeding duodenal ulcer, the endoscopist visualizes a spurting arterial vessel (Forrest Ia); dual therapy with dilute epinephrine and through-the-scope hemoclips achieves complete haemostasis.

page.mentor_intro: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB)—defined as bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz—is a common medical emergency carrying an overall mortality of 5-10%. Etiologies are broadly categorized into non-variceal (peptic ulcer disease [~50%], gastroduodenal erosions, Mallory-Weiss syndrome, Dieulafoy lesions, vascular ectasias, malignancy) and variceal bleeding secondary to portal hypertension. Resuscitation must proceed synchronously with risk stratification (Glasgow-Blatchford Score [GBS]), restrictive blood transfusion, empiric pharmacotherapies, and diagnostic/therapeutic upper endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation.

teaching_points.claim: The Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) is the recommended risk stratification tool for acute UGIB; patients with a GBS of 0-1 have a <1% risk of intervention or death and can safely be managed as outpatients without hospital admission.

A restrictive red blood cell transfusion strategy (transfusing when haemoglobin is <70 g/L [7.0 g/dL], targeting a post-transfusion Hb of 70-90 g/L) significantly reduces rebleeding and all-cause 45-day mortality compared to a liberal strategy (Hb trigger <90 g/L), except in patients with acute coronary syndromes (Villanueva trial).

Intravenous proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy (e.g., omeprazole 80 mg IV bolus followed by 8 mg/h continuous infusion, or 40 mg IV twice daily) raises gastric pH >=6, promoting platelet aggregation and stabilizing fibrin clots in bleeding peptic ulcers.

In patients with suspected variceal haemorrhage or known cirrhosis, empiric vasoactive therapy (terlipressin, octreotide) and prophylactic intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone 1 g daily) must be started immediately upon hospital presentation prior to endoscopy.

Timing of endoscopy: endoscopy should be performed within 24 hours of presentation following hemodynamic resuscitation; emergent endoscopy within <6 hours has not been shown to improve clinical outcomes or reduce mortality in unselected patients.

uncertainties: High-dose continuous IV PPI infusion (80 mg bolus + 8 mg/h) versus intermittent high-dose IV boluses (40 mg IV twice daily) for post-endoscopic high-risk ulcer bleeding.
Optimal timing for restarting oral anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy following endoscopically confirmed haemostasis in high thrombotic risk patients.
mcq_angles: Villanueva restrictive transfusion trial findings: Hb threshold of <70 g/L improves survival and lowers rebleeding in acute upper GI bleeding compared to liberal transfusion (<90 g/L).
Glasgow-Blatchford Score cutoff: identifying scores 0-1 as safe for immediate outpatient discharge.
Endoscopy timing: within 24 hours after resuscitation; ultra-early endoscopy (<6 hours) confers no added mortality benefit.
case_hooks: A 72-year-old woman with osteoarthritis on meloxicam presents with melaena and lightheadedness; BP is 98/62 mmHg, HR 105 bpm, Hb 68 g/L; she receives IV crystalloids, 1 unit of packed RBCs, and IV omeprazole.
A 24-year-old male presents with painless melaena after binge drinking; his GBS is 1; the emergency physician safely discharges him with outpatient follow-up and oral PPI.

page.mentor_intro: Uraemia is the toxic syndrome resulting from the accumulation of organic waste products and nitrogenous metabolites (uraemic retention solutes) normally cleared by healthy kidneys, developing in advanced acute kidney injury or stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CKD). Uraemic toxicity affects virtually every organ system, manifesting as uraemic encephalopathy (asterixis, cognitive blunting, seizures), uraemic pericarditis (friction rub, tamponade risk), uraemic coagulopathy (platelet dysfunction), and uraemic cardiomyopathy. Certain uraemic complications represent absolute, life-threatening indications for emergent renal replacement therapy (haemodialysis), overriding conservative medical stabilization.

teaching_points.claim: Absolute emergent indications for renal replacement therapy (haemodialysis) in acute or chronic kidney failure are remembered by the AEIOU mnemonic: Acidosis (refractory metabolic pH <7.1-7.2), Electrolytes (severe refractory hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L), Ingestion/toxins, Overload (refractory pulmonary oedema), and Uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding).

Uraemic pericarditis presents with retrosternal chest pain and a pericardial friction rub; unlike typical viral pericarditis, ECG often shows NO ST-segment elevation due to lack of epicardial myocardial involvement; it is an absolute indication for urgent haemodialysis (anticoagulation/heparin must be avoided during dialysis to prevent haemorrhagic tamponade).

Uraemic coagulopathy is characterized by abnormal platelet aggregation and adhesion due to impaired von Willebrand factor interaction with dysfunctional platelet GPIIb/IIIa receptors, presenting as bleeding with normal platelet count but prolonged bleeding time.

Desmopressin (DDAVP, 0.3 ug/kg IV or subcutaneous) is the fastest-acting agent to reverse uraemic bleeding prior to urgent invasive procedures (e.g., kidney biopsy), releasing endothelial stores of vWF and factor VIII within 30-60 minutes.

uncertainties: Mechanisms of uraemic cardiomyopathy and reversal of myocardial fibrosis following renal transplantation versus intensive haemodialysis.
Role of Middle Molecules (e.g., beta-2 microglobulin, FGF-23, indoxyl sulfate) clearance with expanded hemodialysis (HDx) and online hemodiafiltration.
mcq_angles: Absolute indications for emergent dialysis: identifying uraemic pericarditis or encephalopathy as mandates for urgent dialysis regardless of exact serum creatinine level.
Acute management of uraemic bleeding diathesis prior to invasive surgery: administration of DDAVP (desmopressin), cryoprecipitate, or conjugated estrogens.
Why systemic anticoagulation is held or minimized during haemodialysis in patients with uraemic pericarditis (preventing conversion into haemorrhagic pericardial tamponade).
case_hooks: A 48-year-old male with untreated ESRD presents with confusion, lethargy, asterixis, and a loud triphasic friction rub over the left sternal border; ECG is non-diagnostic; urgent nephrology consult for dialysis is requested.
A patient with stage 5 CKD is scheduled for an urgent percutaneous kidney biopsy; the nephrologist prescribes pre-procedure DDAVP (0.3 ug/kg) to correct uraemic platelet dysfunction.

page.mentor_intro: Effective long-term management of gout requires treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy (ULT) to promote monosodium urate crystal dissolution, prevent recurrent acute flares, and resolve tophaceous deposits. Stepwise dose titration and concomitant flare prophylaxis are essential for successful treatment.

teaching_points.claim: Allopurinol is the preferred first-line urate-lowering therapy for all patients, starting at a low dose (<=100 mg/day, or <=50 mg/day in chronic kidney disease stage 3-5) and titrated upward every 2 to 4 weeks based on serial serum urate measurements to achieve target levels.

Treat-to-target serum urate thresholds are <6.0 mg/dL (<360 umol/L) for all gout patients to prevent crystal formation, and a more stringent target of <5.0 mg/dL (<300 umol/L) for patients with severe tophaceous gout, chronic erosive arthropathy, or frequent flares.

Concomitant anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis (colchicine 0.5 mg once or twice daily, or low-dose NSAIDs) is strongly recommended when initiating or titrating urate-lowering therapy and should be continued for at least 3 to 6 months to prevent mobilization flares.

Prior to starting allopurinol, HLA-B*58:01 allele screening is recommended in high-risk populations (individuals of Han Chinese, Korean, Thai, or African American descent) due to a dramatically elevated risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS/SJS/TEN); febuxostat serves as an alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor.

uncertainties: Cardiovascular safety profile of febuxostat compared to allopurinol in patients with preexisting severe cardiovascular disease (CARES vs FAST trial discrepancies).
Optimal duration of flare prophylaxis following complete clinical dissolution of all palpable tophi.
mcq_angles: Titration in renal impairment: allopurinol can be safely titrated above conventional renal doses (beyond 300 mg daily) with gradual dose escalations and close monitoring.
Pharmacogenetic screening: HLA-B*58:01 screening prevents life-threatening allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions.
Initiation timing during acute gout flare: ULT can be started during an active flare provided effective anti-inflammatory therapy has been initiated.
case_hooks: A 54-year-old man of Han Chinese descent with recurrent podagra and palpable olecranon tophi, evaluated for urate-lowering therapy initiation.
A 68-year-old man with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min) and chronic tophaceous gout whose serum urate remains 8.8 mg/dL on allopurinol 100 mg daily.

page.mentor_intro: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) represent one of the most frequent bacterial infections encountered in clinical practice, spanning acute uncomplicated cystitis, complicated UTI, catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI), and acute pyelonephritis. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) accounts for >75-85% of community-acquired infections, expressing type 1 and P-fimbriae that mediate uroepithelial adherence and invasion. Diagnostic accuracy requires integrating clinical symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency) with urinalysis (pyuria, nitrite); asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) must be recognized and not treated in non-pregnant, non-urologic surgery populations.

teaching_points.claim: First-line empirical antimicrobial agents for acute uncomplicated cystitis in women include: nitrofurantoin (100 mg orally bid for 5 days), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160/800 mg bid for 3 days, where local resistance is <20%), or fosfomycin trometamol (3 g single oral dose).

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) should NOT be used for uncomplicated cystitis due to serious risks of tendonitis, aortic dissection, peripheral neuropathy, and accelerating population-level antimicrobial resistance; they must be reserved for pyelonephritis or complicated infections.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB)—isolation of significant bacterial count in the absence of symptoms referable to the urinary tract—should ONLY be screened and treated in: (1) pregnant women (to prevent pyelonephritis and low birth weight), and (2) patients undergoing invasive urological procedures with anticipated mucosal bleeding.

Urine dipstick testing: leukocyte esterase indicates the presence of white blood cells (pyuria, ~80-90% sensitivity); nitrite testing indicates enterobacteria that reduce dietary nitrate to nitrite (high specificity >95% but lower sensitivity ~50%).

Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) requires the presence of symptoms with >=10^3 CFU/mL; when CAUTI is diagnosed, replacing or removing the indwelling catheter prior to starting antibiotics accelerates resolution and eradicates intraluminal biofilms.

uncertainties: Clinical utility and threshold of urinary biomarkers (interleukin-6, urinary lactoferrin) in differentiating ASB from symptomatic UTI in patients with advanced dementia.
Efficacy of non-antibiotic bladder instillations (e.g., bacteriophage therapy) in recurrent multidrug-resistant complicated UTIs.
mcq_angles: Indications for treating asymptomatic bacteriuria: pregnancy and pre-urologic mucosal procedures ONLY.
First-line antibiotics and durations for uncomplicated cystitis: nitrofurantoin 5 days vs TMP-SMX 3 days vs fosfomycin single dose.
Why fluoroquinolones are restricted and avoided in simple uncomplicated cystitis (FDA/EMA safety warnings and antimicrobial stewardship).
case_hooks: A 24-year-old healthy female presents with 2 days of painful dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic discomfort without fever or back pain; urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites; nitrofurantoin 100 mg bid for 5 days is prescribed.

An 80-year-old asymptomatic nursing home resident undergoes routine urine dipstick showing positive leukocytes and nitrates, with culture growing 10^5 CFU/mL E. coli; the physician appropriately withholds antibiotic therapy.

page.mentor_intro: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) represent an ascending spectrum of microbial colonization extending from cystitis (bladder mucosal inflammation) to acute pyelonephritis (infection of the renal pelvis and kidney parenchyma). Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) causes >75-80% of infections, with Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, and Enterococcus faecalis accounting for remaining cases. Clinical evaluation hinges on differentiating cystitis (dysuria, urgency, frequency, suprapubic pain without systemic signs) from pyelonephritis (fever, chills, flank/costovertebral angle tenderness, nausea), which mandates systemic antimicrobials and exclusion of obstructive uropathy.

teaching_points.claim: Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis presents with systemic manifestations: fever (>38 C), rigors, costovertebral angle tenderness, and flank pain; urine culture with antimicrobial susceptibility testing is mandatory in all suspected pyelonephritis cases.

First-line outpatient empirical oral therapy for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in regions with local fluoroquinolone resistance <10% is ciprofloxacin (500 mg bid for 7 days) or levofloxacin (750 mg daily for 5 days); if resistance is >=10%, an initial dose of IV ceftriaxone 1 g is required.

Renal imaging (contrast-enhanced CT or renal ultrasound) is NOT routinely required in uncomplicated pyelonephritis that improves within 48-72 hours, but is urgently indicated for persistent fever beyond 72 hours, septic shock, palpable flank mass, or suspected stone obstruction.

Obstructive pyelonephritis (infected hydronephrosis secondary to an obstructing ureteral calculus) is a urologic emergency requiring immediate urinary tract decompression (percutaneous nephrostomy or JJ ureteral stenting) and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.

uncertainties: Oral step-down treatment duration for multi-drug resistant ESBL pyelonephritis using oral fosfomycin or oral carbapenems (tebipenem).
Predictive value of serum procalcitonin versus CRP in guiding early antibiotic cessation in hospitalized pyelonephritis.
mcq_angles: Outpatient antibiotic duration for acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 7 days for oral ciprofloxacin vs 14 days for oral beta-lactams (e.g., augmentin or cephalosporins).
Indications for urgent imaging (contrast CT of abdomen/pelvis) in pyelonephritis: failure to defervesce after 72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy (evaluating renal or perinephric abscess).
Management of pyelonephritis in pregnancy: mandatory hospital admission for parenteral antibiotics (e.g., IV ceftriaxone) due to high risk of sepsis and preterm labour.
case_hooks: A 24-year-old healthy woman presents with temperature 39.1 C, right costovertebral angle tenderness, vomiting, and pyuria; she is initiated on outpatient oral ciprofloxacin after an initial IV ceftriaxone dose.

A 58-year-old diabetic male treated for pyelonephritis with IV ceftriaxone remains febrile with persistent left flank pain on day 4; renal CT reveals a 4 cm intrarenal fluid collection consistent with a renal abscess.

page.mentor_intro: Accurate classification of urinary tract infections dictates diagnostic workup, choice of empirical antibiotics, and treatment duration. Uncomplicated cystitis occurs in non-pregnant, immunocompetent premenopausal adult women without anatomical or functional urinary abnormalities. Complicated UTIs (cUTIs) occur in the presence of factors that compromise host defenses or increase infection severity: male sex, pregnancy, catheterization, urologic instrumentation, neurogenic bladder, urinary tract stones, or immunosuppression, carrying higher rates of multidrug-resistant pathogens.

teaching_points.claim: Uncomplicated cystitis first-line therapies include: nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals (100 mg bid for 5 days), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160/800 mg bid for 3 days, if local resistance <20%), or fosfomycin trometamol (3 g single oral dose); fluoroquinolones are explicitly not recommended for uncomplicated cystitis.

Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) is defined by presence of symptoms referable to the urinary tract (fever, suprapubic pain, altered mental status) with urine culture >=10^3 CFU/mL in a patient with a current or recently removed (<48 h) indwelling catheter; asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in catheterized patients must NOT be treated.

When treating CAUTI, the indwelling urinary catheter must be removed or replaced prior to initiating antibiotic therapy if it has been in place for >7-14 days, as intraluminal biofilms harbor persistent bacterial colonies that prevent cure.

Treatment duration guidelines recommend short-course therapy: 3 to 5 days for uncomplicated cystitis, 7 days for uncomplicated pyelonephritis (fluoroquinolones), 7 days for prompt-responding cUTI/CAUTI, and 14 days for men with suspected acute bacterial prostatitis.

uncertainties: Efficacy of short 7-day courses versus traditional 14-day courses for complicated UTI in male patients with controlled lower urinary tract symptoms.

Role of novel siderophore cephalosporins (cefiderocol) and beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations (ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam) in complicated UTIs due to carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae.
mcq_angles: Appropriate antibiotic treatment durations: 5 days for nitrofurantoin, 3 days for TMP-SMX, 1 single dose for fosfomycin in uncomplicated cystitis.
Management of asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients: withholding antibiotics except in pregnancy or prior to urologic instrumentation with anticipated mucosal bleeding.
Management of CAUTI: mandatory replacement or removal of the catheter before starting targeted antimicrobial therapy.
case_hooks: A 29-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with 2 days of burning dysuria and frequency; urine dipstick is leukocyte esterase and nitrite positive; the clinician selects nitrofurantoin 100 mg bid for 5 days.

A 72-year-old nursing home resident with a long-term Foley catheter has cloudy, foul-smelling urine and a urine culture growing 10^5 CFU/mL Klebsiella; he has no fever, flank pain, or systemic symptoms.

page.mentor_intro: Urticaria is a mast cell-driven dermatological disorder characterized by the rapid appearance of pruritic wheals (hives), angioedema, or both. Wheals feature three distinct hallmarks: central swelling of variable size surrounded by reflex erythema, intense pruritus or burning, and transient nature (individual lesions resolve completely within 24 hours without leaving bruising or hyperpigmentation). Urticaria is classified into acute (<6 weeks) and chronic (>=6 weeks), with chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) driven by mast cell activation through autoallergic (IgE against autoantigens) or autoimmune (IgG against Fc-epsilon-RI or IgE) mechanisms.

teaching_points.claim: Individual urticarial wheals are characteristically transient, resolving within 2 to 24 hours; individual lesions that persist in the exact same location for >24-48 hours, especially with purpura, hyperpigmentation, or burning rather than itching, suggest urticarial vasculitis and mandate skin biopsy.

Step 1 treatment for both acute and chronic urticaria is a standard-dose second-generation H1-antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine, fexofenadine, bilastine, loratadine); first-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) are discouraged due to sedation, anticholinergic toxicity, and REM sleep disruption.

In chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) unresponsive to standard-dose antihistamines after 2-4 weeks, Step 2 guidelines recommend increasing the dose of the second-generation H1-antihistamine up to 4-fold the licensed dose before switching to alternative classes.

For CSU refractory to high-dose antihistamines (Step 3), omalizumab (anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks) is the preferred targeted biologic, achieving complete control in >65-70% of patients with an outstanding safety profile.
Step 4 in the international algorithm is oral cyclosporine (3.5-5 mg/kg daily) for omalizumab-refractory disease, requiring blood pressure and renal function monitoring.

uncertainties: Biomarkers predicting rapid versus slow or poor response to omalizumab (baseline total IgE levels, anti-TPO autoantibody status, basophil activation test).
Comparative efficacy of emerging oral Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors (remibrutinib, fenebrutinib) versus injectable biologics in CSU.
mcq_angles: Transient nature of true urticarial wheals (<24 hours) versus urticarial vasculitis (>24 hours with post-inflammatory purpura/staining).
Stepwise international guidelines for CSU: up-dosing second-generation H1-antihistamines up to 4x standard dose before adding omalizumab.
Disadvantages of first-generation sedating antihistamines (cognitive impairment, anticholinergic side effects) establishing second-generation agents as undisputed first-line.
case_hooks: A 30-year-old woman presents with daily itchy wheals across her trunk and limbs for 10 weeks; individual lesions disappear within 12 hours; she has inadequate control on fexofenadine 180 mg daily; the dose is increased to 360 mg twice daily.
A 45-year-old male presents with hives that each remain fixed for 36 hours and leave faint purpuric staining; skin punch biopsy demonstrates leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
