page.mentor_intro: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) is a benign, slow-growing neoplasm arising from the Schwann cell sheath of the superior or inferior vestibular branch of the eighth cranial nerve (CN VIII) within the internal auditory canal (IAC) and cerebellopontine angle (CPA). Sporadic tumours are typically unilateral and present in the fifth to sixth decades, whereas bilateral vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic for Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2-related schwannomatosis, caused by NF2 tumour suppressor gene mutations on chromosome 22q12). Management decisions—surveillance ('wait-and-scan'), stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS), or microsurgical resection—depend on tumour size (Koos classification), hearing status, brainstem compression, and patient age.

teaching_points.claim: The classic triad of symptoms includes progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, asymmetrical tinnitus, and unsteadiness; high-resolution contrast-enhanced brain MRI (T1 with gadolinium through the posterior fossa and thin-slice CISS/FIESTA) is the gold standard diagnostic imaging.

Initial observation with serial MRI ('wait-and-scan' protocol every 6-12 months) is the preferred primary strategy for small, intracanalicular tumours (<1.5 cm) or asymptomatic lesions in older adults, as up to 50% demonstrate no measurable growth over several years.

Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS, e.g., Gamma Knife, single fraction <=12-13 Gy to margin) provides excellent long-term local tumour control (>90-95%) with low facial nerve injury risk (<1%) for small-to-medium tumours (<2.5-3.0 cm) without significant brainstem compression.

Microsurgical resection (translabyrinthine, retrosigmoid, or middle cranial fossa approach) is indicated for large tumours (Koos Grade IV, >3 cm) causing brainstem displacement, progressive obstructive hydrocephalus, or intractable trigeminal neuropathy.

In Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2), bilateral vestibular schwannomas cause inevitable bilateral profound deafness; bevacizumab (anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody) is an evidence-based medical therapy that halts tumour progression and preserves or improves hearing in up to 40-50% of NF2 patients.

uncertainties: Long-term risk of secondary radiation-induced malignant transformation (malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour) following stereotactic radiosurgery in young patients and NF2 patients.
Optimal timing of auditory brainstem implant (ABI) versus cochlear implant (CI) in NF2 patients undergoing vestibular schwannoma removal.
mcq_angles: Pathognomonic criterion for Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2): bilateral vestibular schwannomas on neuroimaging.
Comparing surgical approaches: translabyrinthine approach guarantees complete hearing sacrifice but minimizes brain retraction; retrosigmoid allows potential hearing preservation.
Role of bevacizumab in NF2: medical management to reduce tumour volume and preserve hearing without surgery.
case_hooks: A 52-year-old male presents with gradual hearing loss in his left ear and difficulty understanding telephone speech; audiogram shows high-frequency asymmetric sensorineural loss; MRI demonstrates an 8 mm left intracanalicular mass.

A 21-year-old woman with known NF2 presents with bilateral vestibular schwannomas (1.8 cm right, 2.2 cm left); she has rapidly deteriorating speech discrimination in her remaining functional ear; bevacizumab therapy is initiated.

page.mentor_intro: VEXAS syndrome (Vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, Autoinflammatory, Somatic) is a severe, life-threatening adult-onset autoinflammatory and haematologic disorder described in 2020. It is caused by acquired somatic missense mutations in the UBA1 gene on the X chromosome (most commonly affecting codon 41: p.Met41Thr, p.Met41Val, p.Met41Leu) within haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, predominantly affecting men aged >50 years. VEXAS manifests as a devastating overlap of systemic inflammation (relapsing polychondritis, chondritis of ears/nose, neutrophilic dermatoses, pulmonary infiltrates, fever, venous thromboembolism) and haematologic abnormalities (macrocytic anaemia, myelodysplastic syndrome [MDS], and characteristic bone marrow proerythroblast cytoplasmic vacuoles).

teaching_points.claim: VEXAS syndrome is caused by somatic mutations in the UBA1 gene (encoding the ubiquitin-activating enzyme E1), affecting haematopoietic stem cells and causing defective ubiquitination and systemic autoinflammation.

Clinical presentation classically mimics multiple rheumatologic diseases: relapsing polychondritis (ear/nose chondritis sparing earlobes), Sweet syndrome, polyarteritis nodosa, pulmonary infiltrates, recurrent unprovoked venous thromboembolism, and fever, refractory to standard DMARDs.

Haematologic hallmarks include progressive macrocytic anaemia (elevated MCV), thrombocytopenia, myelodysplastic syndrome, and pathognomonic cytoplasmic vacuoles in erythroid and myeloid precursor cells on bone marrow aspirate.

Definitive diagnosis requires targeted genetic sequencing (Sanger sequencing or NGS) demonstrating somatic UBA1 variants in peripheral blood or bone marrow; high-dose corticosteroids achieve initial symptom control, while hypomethylating agents (azacitidine), JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib), and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) offer targeted therapy.

uncertainties: Optimal patient selection, conditioning regimens, and transplant-related mortality of allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation in elderly VEXAS patients.
Comparative long-term clinical response between azacitidine and JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib, tofacitinib) in delaying progression to bone marrow failure.
mcq_angles: Genetic basis and inheritance: VEXAS is an acquired somatic mutation in UBA1 on the X chromosome, NOT an inherited germline defect.
Pathognomonic bone marrow biopsy finding: cytoplasmic vacuolization of myeloid and erythroid precursor cells.
Therapeutic escalation in steroid-refractory VEXAS: utilizing azacitidine (hypomethylating agent) or JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib), and curative potential of allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

A bone marrow biopsy in an elderly male with suspected myelodysplasia reveals abundant prominent intracytoplasmic vacuoles in pronormoblasts and early myeloid cells; peripheral blood NGS confirms a UBA1 p.Met41Thr mutation.

page.mentor_intro: Viral encephalitis is a medical and neurological emergency characterized by acute inflammation of the brain parenchyma, manifesting as altered mental status, fever, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is the most frequent and devastating cause of sporadic viral encephalitis in adults, carrying an untreated mortality of >70% with devastating permanent neurocognitive sequelae. Immediate empirical intravenous acyclovir must be instituted upon the earliest clinical suspicion without waiting for lumbar puncture results or neuroimaging, as treatment delay directly correlates with fatal outcomes and catastrophic permanent brain necrosis.

teaching_points.claim: Empirical intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours, adjusted for renal function) must be administered IMMEDIATELY to any patient presenting with acute encephalopathy and fever, prior to or concurrently with diagnostic lumbar puncture and brain MRI.

CSF analysis classically reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis (50-500 WBC/uL), elevated protein (0.6-1.5 g/L), normal glucose (CSF-to-serum ratio >0.5), and frequently elevated red blood cells reflecting necrotizing haemorrhagic encephalitis.

CSF HSV-1 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the gold standard diagnostic test (>95% sensitivity and specificity); however, testing performed within the first 24-48 hours can yield false-negative results; if clinical suspicion remains high, acyclovir must be continued and CSF PCR repeated at 3 to 7 days.

Brain MRI is the neuroimaging modality of choice, characteristically demonstrating hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences with restricted diffusion restricted to the temporal lobes, insular cortex, and inferior frontal lobes (frequently asymmetric).

Intravenous acyclovir therapy for confirmed HSV encephalitis must be continued for a full 14 to 21 days; acyclovir can precipitate crystal nephropathy and acute tubular obstruction, requiring adequate pre-hydration and renal function monitoring.

uncertainties: Role of adjunctive systemic corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) alongside acyclovir in reducing cerebral edema and long-term neurocognitive impairment.
Diagnostic yield and turnaround impact of metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) in suspected infectious encephalitis with negative standard viral PCR panels.
mcq_angles: Emergency management priority: starting empiric IV acyclovir immediately upon presentation before neuroimaging or LP.
Characteristic brain MRI distribution of HSV-1 encephalitis: bilateral asymmetric temporal and frontobasal cortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensity.
Handling early negative CSF HSV PCR: recognizing false-negative results in the first 24-48 hours and continuing acyclovir with repeat LP in 3-7 days.
case_hooks: A 46-year-old male is brought to the ED with acute confusion, fever of 38.9 C, aphasia, and a focal motor seizure; non-contrast head CT is unremarkable; the physician immediately begins IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg.
A patient with confirmed HSV-1 encephalitis receives IV acyclovir; on day 4, serum creatinine rises from 85 to 210 umol/L; urine microscopy shows needle-shaped birefrigent acyclovir crystals.

page.mentor_intro: Viral haemorrhagic fevers (VHFs)—encompassing Filoviruses (Ebola, Marburg), Arenaviruses (Lassa fever), Bunyavirales (Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever), and Flaviviruses (Yellow fever, severe Dengue)—are high-consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) capable of causing catastrophic multi-organ failure and nosocomial dissemination. Pathophysiology involves viral tropism for endothelial cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells, triggering massive pro-inflammatory cytokine release, microvascular leakage, consumptive coagulopathy, and profound hypovolemic/distributive shock. ICU management demands strict biosafety containment, aggressive volume resuscitation, organ support, and rapid deployment of targeted therapeutics (monoclonal antibodies for Ebola, intravenous ribavirin for Lassa fever).

teaching_points.claim: Infection prevention and control is paramount: strict biosafety Level 4 precautions or specialized High-Level Isolation Units (HLIU) with full personal protective equipment (PPE: powered air-purifying respirators [PAPRs] or fluid-resistant coveralls with double gloving, N95/FFP3 respirators, and chemical-resistant boots) with trained observers for donning/doffing.

Severe Ebola virus disease (EVD) typically manifests with massive gastrointestinal volume loss (severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting up to 5-10 L/day), causing profound hypovolemia, electrolyte wasting (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia), metabolic acidosis, and prerenal AKI requiring aggressive point-of-care-guided fluid replacement.

Monoclonal antibody therapies—specifically Inmazeb (atoltivimab, maftivimab, and odesivimab-ebgn cocktail) and Ebanga (ansuvimab-zykw)—significantly reduce 28-day mortality in Ebola virus disease (Zaire ebolavirus) when administered early (PALM randomized trial).

Intravenous ribavirin is the specific antiviral therapy of choice for Lassa fever and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, demonstrating significant mortality reduction when initiated within the first 6 days of illness onset.

uncertainties: Efficacy of novel broad-spectrum antivirals (remdesivir, favipiravir) across diverse filovirus species (e.g., Sudan virus, Marburg virus) where specific monoclonal antibodies are ineffective.
Safety and optimal delivery of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and mechanical ventilation in high-level biocontainment environments.
mcq_angles: Specific antiviral treatments by VHF family: monoclonal antibodies (Inmazeb, Ebanga) for Ebola vs intravenous ribavirin for Lassa fever.
Primary mechanism of death in severe Ebola virus disease: profound hypovolemic shock and electrolyte collapse from massive gastrointestinal fluid losses.
Personal protective equipment protocol: mandatory use of trained buddy observers during doffing to eliminate self-contamination.

page.mentor_intro: Viral hepatitis A and E: faeco-oral transmission, self-limiting, vaccination, fulminant hepatitis is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

teaching_points.claim: Contemporary evidence synthesis highlights core pathophysiology, clinical staging, and multidisciplinary management: Genetic and autoimmune predispositions to fulminant viral hepatitis in children.

Hepatitis A (HAV) and Hepatitis E (HEV genotypes 1 and 2) are transmitted primarily via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food and water, causing acute self-limiting hepatitis diagnosed by serum IgM antibodies.
Hepatitis E infection during pregnancy (especially in the third trimester with genotypes 1 and 2) carries a devastating risk of fulminant hepatic failure and maternal mortality approaching 20-25%.

In solid organ transplant recipients and immunosuppressed individuals, HEV (genotype 3) can cause chronic hepatitis and rapid progression to cirrhosis, requiring reduction in immunosuppression and treatment with oral ribavirin.

page.mentor_intro: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a partially double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Hepadnaviridae family, transmitted via perinatal, percutaneous, or sexual exposure. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB)—defined by persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for >=6 months—affects over 250 million people worldwide, leading to cirrhosis, liver failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Serological interpretation of HBV markers (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc IgM/IgG, HBeAg, anti-HBe, and quantitative HBV DNA) establishes disease phase and directs potent, high barrier-to-resistance nucleos(t)ide analogue antiviral therapy (entecavir, tenofovir).

teaching_points.claim: Serological interpretation: HBsAg indicates active infection (acute or chronic); anti-HBs indicates immunity (from vaccination if isolated, or natural recovery if combined with anti-HBc IgG); anti-HBc IgM indicates acute infection; and HBeAg correlates with high viral replication and infectivity.

First-line antiviral therapies for chronic hepatitis B are nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high genetic barrier to resistance: entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF); lamivudine and adefovir are abandoned due to high resistance rates.

Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) delivers equivalent viral suppression to TDF with significantly improved renal (less tubular proteinuria and GFR decline) and bone mineral density safety profiles, making TAF or entecavir preferred in patients aged >60 years, with CKD, or with osteoporosis.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) screening with abdominal ultrasound every 6 months (with or without serum alpha-fetoprotein [AFP]) is mandatory in all cirrhotic patients, Asian men >40 years, Asian women >50 years, African patients >20 years, and those with a family history of HCC, even in non-cirrhotic patients with suppressed viral loads.

Prophylactic antiviral therapy (entecavir or tenofovir) is mandatory before initiating B-cell depleting therapies (rituximab) or intensive chemotherapy in patients who are HBsAg-positive or anti-HBc positive (even if HBsAg-negative), to prevent life-threatening HBV reactivation and fulminant hepatic failure.

uncertainties: Feasibility and safety of discontinuing nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy in HBeAg-negative patients with sustained viral suppression ('stopping rules' to achieve functional cure).
Role of novel therapeutic pipelines (siRNA gene silencers, capsid assembly modulators, entry inhibitors) in achieving functional cure (sustained HBsAg seroclearance).
mcq_angles: Deciphering HBV serology panels: distinguishing vaccine-induced immunity (anti-HBs alone) from resolved natural infection (anti-HBs + anti-HBc IgG).
Selecting TAF or entecavir over TDF in patients with baseline chronic kidney disease or osteopenia to avoid proximal renal tubulopathy and bone loss.
Preventing HBV reactivation during immunosuppression: universal screening with HBsAg and anti-HBc and preemptive antiviral prophylaxis during rituximab therapy.
case_hooks: A 34-year-old asymptomatic male has HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgG positive, HBeAg positive, HBV DNA 12,000,000 IU/mL, and ALT 95 U/L; he is initiated on oral entecavir 0.5 mg daily.

A 62-year-old woman with lymphoma is scheduled for R-CHOP chemotherapy; screening reveals HBsAg negative but anti-HBc IgG positive; she is started on prophylactic entecavir to prevent lethal viral reactivation.

page.mentor_intro: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a single-stranded enveloped RNA flavivirus transmitted predominantly through parenteral blood exposure (injection drug use, unsterilized medical equipment, blood transfusions prior to 1992). Unlike HBV, acute HCV rarely resolves spontaneously (75-85% progress to chronic hepatitis C), leading silently over decades to progressive liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, end-stage liver disease, and hepatocellular carcinoma. The advent of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy has revolutionized medicine: pangenotypic, all-oral, interferon-free regimens administered for 8 to 12 weeks achieve sustained virological response (SVR12 / virological cure) in >95-98% of patients with minimal adverse effects.

teaching_points.claim: Diagnostic confirmation of active hepatitis C infection requires a two-step algorithm: screening with anti-HCV antibody (demonstrating exposure) followed by mandatory reflexive HCV RNA PCR testing to confirm active viral replication.

Sustained Virological Response (SVR12, defined as undetectable serum HCV RNA at 12 weeks after completing antiviral therapy) represents a definitive microbiological cure, associated with halted fibrosis progression, reduced portal hypertension, and >70% reduction in hepatocellular carcinoma and all-cause mortality.

First-line treatment utilizes all-oral, pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens: glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (3 tablets daily with food for 8 weeks in treatment-naive non-cirrhotic patients) or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (1 tablet daily for 12 weeks), effective across all HCV genotypes 1 through 6.

Drug-drug interactions with DAAs are common: sofosbuvir is contraindicated with amiodarone (causes life-threatening symptomatic bradycardia and fatal cardiac arrest); acid-reducing agents (PPIs) impair velpatasvir absorption; and statins require dose adjustments with protease inhibitors (glecaprevir).

Patients who achieve SVR but have pre-existing advanced fibrosis (F3) or cirrhosis (F4) remain at permanent lifetime risk for hepatocellular carcinoma and must continue lifelong surveillance with abdominal ultrasound every 6 months.

uncertainties: Optimal salvage regimens for the rare <2-3% of patients failing first-line pangenotypic DAAs (triple-combination sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir for 12 weeks).
Reinfection rates and public health micro-elimination strategies among active injection drug users and incarcerated populations.
mcq_angles: Confirming active HCV infection: why positive anti-HCV antibody must always be followed by quantitative HCV RNA PCR testing.
Lethal drug-drug interaction: co-administration of sofosbuvir and amiodarone is strictly contraindicated due to severe bradyarrhythmias.
Post-cure surveillance: patients with pre-existing cirrhosis (F4) who achieve SVR12 still require lifelong semi-annual ultrasound HCC screening.
case_hooks: A 44-year-old male with a history of injection drug use tests positive for anti-HCV; reflexive HCV RNA is 1,800,000 IU/mL (Genotype 3); transient elastography shows F1 fibrosis; he is cured with 8 weeks of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir.

A 60-year-old cirrhotic patient achieves SVR12 after sofosbuvir/velpatasvir; the patient asks if routine follow-up can be discontinued; the hepatologist explains the necessity of ongoing 6-monthly liver ultrasound for HCC screening.

page.mentor_intro: Viral-induced arthritides are acute, self-limiting or chronic inflammatory joint syndromes triggered by systemic viral infections. Underlying mechanisms include direct synovial viral invasion, immune complex deposition with complement consumption (Type III hypersensitivity), and molecular mimicry triggering autoimmunity. Classic culprits include Parvovirus B19 (symmetric small joint polyarthritis mimicking early rheumatoid arthritis in adults), Hepatitis B and C, Rubella, and arthropod-borne alphaviruses (Chikungunya, Ross River, Mayaro); distinguishing viral arthritis from emerging autoimmune disease avoids unnecessary immunosuppressive therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum ('fifth disease', slapped-cheek rash) in children, but in adults (especially mothers and schoolteachers) presents as acute symmetric polyarthritis of the small joints of the hands, wrists, and knees, closely mimicking rheumatoid arthritis with positive anti-B19 IgM antibodies.

Hepatitis B virus infection triggers a serum sickness-like prodrome prior to the onset of jaundice, characterized by urticarial rash, angioedema, symmetric polyarthritis, and hypocomplementaemia due to circulating HBsAg-anti-HBs immune complex deposition.

Hepatitis C virus is strongly associated with mixed cryoglobulinaemia (Type II/III), presenting with the classic Meltzer triad of purpura, arthralgias, and asthenia/fatigue, accompanied by positive rheumatoid factor and low C4 levels.

Chikungunya virus (transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes) causes an acute syndrome of high fever, petechial rash, and severe, debilitating, incapacitating polyarthralgias/polyarthritis that can persist chronically in over 30-50% of patients for months to years.

Viral arthritides are generally managed symptomatically with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and paracetamol; systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressives should be strictly avoided in the acute phase as they can impair viral clearance.

uncertainties: Pathophysiological mechanisms governing the transition from acute Chikungunya viremia to chronic, destructive post-viral arthropathy.
Role of temporary low-dose methotrexate or biologics in chronic, refractory Chikungunya arthritis unresponsive to NSAIDs.
mcq_angles: Differentiating Parvovirus B19 polyarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis: sudden onset, exposure to children, spontaneous resolution within 2-6 weeks, and presence of anti-B19 IgM.
Recognizing Hepatitis B serum sickness-like prodrome: acute arthritis, urticaria, low complement (C3/C4) preceding hepatic transaminase elevation.
Mixed cryoglobulinaemia associated with Hepatitis C: low C4, positive RF, purpura, and treatment directed at antiviral cure (direct-acting antivirals [DAAs]).
case_hooks: A 32-year-old primary school teacher presents with sudden bilateral wrist and MCP swelling and morning stiffness 10 days after several students in her class had facial rashes; Parvovirus B19 IgM is positive.

A 45-year-old male with chronic Hepatitis C presents with palpable purpura on both lower legs, arthralgias, and numbness in his feet; laboratory work reveals elevated rheumatoid factor and undetectable serum C4.

page.mentor_intro: Viral respiratory pathogens beyond influenza and SARS-CoV-2—prominently respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human parainfluenza viruses (HPIV), and adenoviruses—cause immense disease burden across extremes of age and in immunocompromised hosts. RSV is the primary cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants and acute cardiopulmonary hospitalization in older adults. Parainfluenza viruses (especially HPIV-1 and HPIV-2) are the classic culprits behind acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup), while adenovirus produces severe pharyngitis, follicular conjunctivitis, pneumonia, and life-threatening disseminated disease in stem cell transplant recipients.

teaching_points.claim: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) manifests in infants as acute bronchiolitis (tachypnoea, wheezing, subcostal retractions, feeding difficulty); in older adults (>=60-65 years) and patients with COPD or congestive heart failure, RSV causes severe lower respiratory tract disease and mortality comparable to non-pandemic influenza.

Passive immunoprophylaxis with nirsevimab (a long-acting monoclonal antibody targeting the prefusion F protein) administered as a single intramuscular injection protects all infants entering their first RSV season; maternal prefusion F bivalent vaccine (Abrysvo) given at 32-36 weeks gestation confers passive transplacental protection.

Human parainfluenza virus (HPIV-1) is the leading cause of viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) in children aged 6 months to 3 years, characterized by a classic 'barking' seal-like cough, inspiratory stridor, and the 'steeple sign' (subglottic tracheal narrowing) on neck radiograph; treatment is oral dexamethasone (0.15-0.60 mg/kg) and nebulized epinephrine for severe distress.

Adenovirus infections in allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients can cause disseminated disease, necrotizing pneumonia, and acute liver failure; quantitative plasma adenovirus PCR is monitored, with intravenous cidofovir (or brincidofovir) used for preemptive or targeted therapy.

uncertainties: Clinical efficacy and renal safety profile of novel investigational oral RSV fusion inhibitors in immunocompromised bone marrow transplant patients.
Efficacy of adoptive virus-specific T-cell (VST) immunotherapy in refractory disseminated adenovirus infections post-transplantation.
mcq_angles: RSV preventative strategies: nirsevimab long-acting monoclonal antibody for infants vs maternal vaccination during weeks 32-36.
Management of acute croup: single dose oral dexamethasone (0.15-0.6 mg/kg) with nebulized racemic epinephrine for resting stridor.
Recognizing life-threatening adenovirus disease in transplant recipients: quantitative plasma PCR monitoring and cidofovir therapy.

A 2-year-old boy presents at 2 AM with a sudden barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor that worsens with crying; neck X-ray demonstrates subglottic narrowing ('steeple sign').

page.mentor_intro: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) and folate (vitamin B9) are essential water-soluble vitamins critical for DNA synthesis, erythropoiesis, and neurological myelin maintenance. Both deficiencies impair pyrimidine synthesis, resulting in nuclear-cytoplasmic dyssynchrony that manifests morphologically as megaloblastic anaemia (macrocytosis, MCV >100-110 fL, and hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear). The critical clinical mandate is never administering folic acid alone for megaloblastic anaemia without first excluding vitamin B12 deficiency; folate corrects the haematologic anaemia but accelerates catastrophic, irreversible neurological degeneration (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord).

teaching_points.claim: Folic acid supplementation must NEVER be given as monotherapy in undiagnosed megaloblastic anaemia without ruling out vitamin B12 deficiency; folate bypasses the thymidylate synthase block to correct haematologic cytopenias while allowing irreversible neurological destruction to progress unchecked.

Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord, characterized by demyelination of the posterior columns (loss of vibration and proprioception, sensory ataxia) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses).

Biochemical differentiation between B12 and folate deficiency uses metabolic intermediates: methylmalonic acid (MMA) is elevated in B12 deficiency but NORMAL in folate deficiency; homocysteine is elevated in BOTH B12 and folate deficiencies.

Pernicious anaemia—an autoimmune gastritis causing intrinsic factor deficiency from destruction of gastric parietal cells—is the leading cause of B12 deficiency in adults, confirmed by positive anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (highly specific) or anti-parietal cell antibodies.

Parenteral vitamin B12 replacement (intramuscular hydroxycobalamin 1000 ug on alternate days until neurological symptoms stabilize, followed by maintenance every 2-3 months) is the standard for pernicious anaemia and patients with neurological involvement.

uncertainties: Clinical equivalence of high-dose oral vitamin B12 (1000-2000 ug daily via passive intestinal diffusion) versus intramuscular injections in patients with severe pernicious anaemia and neurological deficits.
Diagnostic accuracy of serum total B12 versus holotranscobalamin (active B12) in borderline deficiency states.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic biochemical distinction: elevated methylmalonic acid (MMA) confirms B12 deficiency (normal in folate deficiency).
Consequences of administering folic acid monotherapy to a B12-deficient patient (corrects macrocytic anaemia but precipitates/accelerates subacute combined degeneration of the cord).
Specific antibody testing in pernicious anaemia: anti-intrinsic factor antibody (high specificity ~99%) vs anti-parietal cell antibody (high sensitivity ~90% but lower specificity).

page.mentor_intro: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is an essential water-soluble cofactor required for two critical intracellular enzymes: methionine synthase (converting homocysteine to methionine, essential for DNA purine/pyrimidine synthesis and myelin methylation) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (converting methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA). Deficiency leads to defective DNA synthesis, resulting in megaloblastic haematopoiesis (macrocytic anaemia, hypersegmented neutrophils), and progressive demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous systems. Crucially, neuropsychiatric symptoms—paresthesias, sensory ataxia from subacute combined degeneration, spasticity, dementia, depression—can develop in the complete absence of haematologic anaemia.

teaching_points.claim: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause devastating, irreversible neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy, cognitive decline) EVEN IN THE ABSENCE of haematologic anaemia or macrocytosis.

Serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) is the most sensitive and specific functional metabolic biomarker for cellular B12 deficiency, significantly superior to total serum B12; MMA is elevated in B12 deficiency but completely normal in folate deficiency.

Recreational nitrous oxide ('whippits') inhalation is an increasingly recognized cause of acute, severe functional B12 deficiency; nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidizes the cobalt core of cobalamin from Co+ to Co3+, inactivating methionine synthase and precipitating acute myeloneuropathy with normal or borderline serum B12 levels.

Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune atrophic gastritis causing destruction of gastric parietal cells and loss of intrinsic factor secretion, confirmed by testing for anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (specificity ~99%); it carries a 3-fold increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumours.

Treatment of symptomatic B12 deficiency with neurological involvement requires immediate intramuscular hydroxycobalamin (1000 ug on alternate days for 2 weeks or until neurological improvement ceases, followed by maintenance 1000 ug every 2-3 months for life).

uncertainties: Diagnostic thresholds and clinical equivalence of active B12 (holotranscobalamin) compared to total serum cobalamin and methylmalonic acid in primary care.
Efficacy of high-dose oral cobalamin (1000-2000 ug daily via non-intrinsic factor-dependent passive diffusion) in treating subacute combined degeneration compared to parenteral injections.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic utility of methylmalonic acid (MMA): elevated in B12 deficiency, distinguishing it from isolated folate deficiency.
Mechanism of nitrous oxide neurotoxicity: chemical oxidation and functional inactivation of vitamin B12 causing acute subacute combined degeneration.
Administration of folic acid in unrecognized B12 deficiency: resolves haematologic megaloblastic changes while masking and accelerating neurological destruction.

A 68-year-old woman presents with progressive memory loss and bilateral lower limb paresthesias; CBC shows macrocytic anaemia (Hb 92 g/L, MCV 112 fL) with hypersegmented neutrophils; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are positive.

page.mentor_intro: Vitamin D is essential for calcium homeostasis, bone mineralization, and neuromuscular function. Assessment utilizes serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], with treatment strategies stratified by deficiency severity to heal osteomalacia, prevent rickets, and preserve bone mineral density.

teaching_points.claim: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] is the definitive diagnostic marker for evaluating vitamin D status; deficiency is defined as <25-30 nmol/L (<10-12 ng/mL), insufficiency as 30-50 nmol/L (12-20 ng/mL), and sufficiency as >50 nmol/L (>20 ng/mL), with target levels of 75 nmol/L (30 ng/mL) recommended in osteoporosis.

Treatment of symptomatic deficiency or osteomalacia requires high-dose repletion: oral cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) 50,000 IU once weekly (or 300,000 IU total cumulative loading dose divided over 6 to 10 weeks), followed by lifelong daily maintenance dosing of 800 to 2,000 IU daily.

Severe prolonged vitamin D deficiency leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism, hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and defective osteoid mineralization, manifesting as osteomalacia in adults (diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, Waddling gait, pseudo-fractures/Looser zones) and rickets in children.

Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) is preferred over ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) because it maintains serum 25(OH)D concentrations longer and has greater bioefficacy; active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) is indicated only in severe renal failure or 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency, not in nutritional deficiency.

uncertainties: Optimal target 25(OH)D levels for extra-skeletal health benefits (immune modulation, cardiovascular protection, cancer prevention).
Comparative safety and hypercalcemia risk of intermittent high-dose bolus therapy (e.g., annual megadoses) versus daily low-dose maintenance supplementation in fall prevention.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic biomarker selection: measure 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol), not 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), which is often normal or elevated in nutritional deficiency due to secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Radiographic hallmark of osteomalacia: Looser zones (pseudofractures)—transverse cortical radiolucent bands perpendicular to the bone cortex, classically in the femoral neck, pubic rami, or scapula.
Laboratory pattern in osteomalacia: low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate, elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH), and elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP).
case_hooks: A 68-year-old housebound woman presenting with chronic widespread bone pain, difficulty standing from a chair, a serum 25(OH)D of 16 nmol/L, and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
A 32-year-old woman with celiac disease presenting with bilateral groin pain whose pelvic radiographs demonstrate bilateral femoral neck Looser zones.

teaching_points.claim: Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Direct oral anticoagulants versus vitamin K antagonists for postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Switching from Vitamin K Antagonists to Direct Oral Anticoagulants in Frail Elderly Patients with Atrial Fibrillation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

In the landmark BRIDGE randomized trial of patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation receiving warfarin who required temporary interruption for elective procedures, bridging anticoagulation with therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) failed to reduce arterial thromboembolism (0.4% vs 0.3%) and significantly tripled the risk of major bleeding (3.2% vs 1.3%) compared with no bridging, establishing that routine heparin bridging is unnecessary and harmful for standard-risk AF.

In patients with mechanical heart valves, particularly in the mitral position or with older-generation valves, therapeutic LMWH or unfractionated heparin bridging remains recommended perioperatively despite the findings of the BRIDGE trial in non-valvular AF.

page.mentor_intro: Coagulopathy in chronic liver disease was historically viewed as an isolated bleeding diathesis, defined by elevated conventional clotting times (prothrombin time [PT] and international normalized ratio [INR]). Modern haematology recognizes cirrhosis as a state of 'rebalanced haemostasis': concomitant declines in liver-synthesized procoagulant factors (II, VII, IX, X, V) are offset by parallel declines in endogenous anticoagulants (protein C, protein S, antithrombin III) and elevated endothelial von Willebrand factor. Vitamin K deficiency (from malnutrition, prolonged antibiotics, or cholestasis with bile salt deficiency impairing fat-soluble vitamin absorption) must be distinguished from parenchymal hepatic synthetic failure.

teaching_points.claim: Liver disease coagulopathy represents a fragile 'rebalanced haemostasis' where patients have reduced procoagulants but also reduced anticoagulants (protein C, protein S, antithrombin); routine INR reflects ONLY procoagulant factor deficiencies and does NOT accurately predict clinical bleeding risk or protection against thrombosis.

Vitamin K is an essential cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which carboxymates procoagulant factors II, VII, IX, X, and anticoagulant proteins C and S; vitamin K deficiency responds to intravenous vitamin K (10 mg IV), whereas end-stage parenchymal failure does not correct.

Factor V activity testing differentiates vitamin K deficiency from hepatic synthetic failure: Factor V is synthesized by the liver independently of vitamin K; low Factor V indicates genuine parenchymal synthetic failure, whereas normal Factor V with prolonged PT/INR points to pure vitamin K deficiency.

Prophylactic correction of elevated INR using fresh frozen plasma (FFP) prior to low-risk invasive procedures (paracentesis, thoracentesis, endoscopic band ligation) is explicitly not recommended by gastroenterology guidelines, as it increases portal hypertension and circulatory overload without reducing bleeding.

Viscoelastometric testing (thromboelastography [TEG] or rotational thromboelastometry [ROTEM]) provides a comprehensive assessment of whole-blood clot firmness and fibrinolysis, serving as the superior method to guide blood product transfusions in actively bleeding cirrhotic patients.

uncertainties: Safety and efficacy of 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrates (4F-PCC) versus fresh frozen plasma in acute severe bleeding in cirrhosis.
Reliability of viscoelastometric parameters (TEG/ROTEM) in guiding pre-operative optimization prior to major hepatic resection or liver transplantation.
mcq_angles: Differentiating vitamin K deficiency from liver failure using Factor V vs Factor VII (Factor V synthesis is vitamin K-independent).
Why INR cannot be used to predict procedural bleeding risk in cirrhotic patients (rebalanced haemostasis with concurrent protein C/S reduction).
Inappropriateness of routine pre-procedure fresh frozen plasma (FFP) transfusions in stable cirrhosis undergoing paracentesis (increases volume and portal pressure without hemostatic benefit).
case_hooks: A 58-year-old male with biliary obstruction from choledocholithiasis presents with an INR of 2.4; after receiving 10 mg of intravenous phytomenadione (vitamin K1), his INR normalizes to 1.1 within 24 hours.

A patient with decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) has an INR of 2.2 and platelet count 55 x 10^9/L; the surgical resident orders 4 units of FFP before an elective paracentesis, which the attending cancels.

page.mentor_intro: Vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—now formally termed inducible laryngeal obstruction (ILO) or paradoxical vocal fold motion (PVFM)—is characterized by inappropriate, episodic adduction of the vocal cords during respiration, primarily during inspiration. VCD causes acute upper airway obstruction, manifesting as episodic dyspnoea, choking sensations, throat tightness, and inspiratory stridor, frequently triggered by exercise, emotional distress, cold air, or irritants (laryngopharyngeal reflux). Because VCD classically mimics asthma, patients are frequently misdiagnosed for years, receiving escalating high-dose inhaled corticosteroids, systemic steroids, and repeated emergency department visits without clinical improvement.

teaching_points.claim: Vocal cord dysfunction / inducible laryngeal obstruction (VCD/ILO) is defined by paradoxical adduction of the true vocal folds during inspiration, producing acute inspiratory dyspnoea, throat tightness, and stridor; symptoms are unresponsive to inhaled short-acting beta-agonists (albuterol).

The diagnostic gold standard is direct visualization via flexible nasolaryngoscopy during an acute symptomatic episode (or immediately following a provocative trigger, such as continuous exercise testing), documenting >=50% vocal fold adduction during inspiration with posterior chink formation.

Spirometry during an acute episode demonstrates a classic variable extrathoracic upper airway obstruction pattern: marked flattening or truncation of the inspiratory flow-volume loop with a normal expiratory limb.

First-line management centers on specialized speech-language pathology (respiratory retraining therapy, quick-release rescue breathing techniques: pursed-lip breathing, sniff-puffs, diaphragmatic breathing) and treating concurrent triggers (gastroesophageal/laryngopharyngeal reflux and post-nasal drip).

uncertainties: Diagnostic sensitivity and concordance of continuous laryngoscopy during exercise (CLE) testing versus post-exercise laryngoscopy.
Role of laryngeal botulinum toxin (Botox) injections into the thyroarytenoid muscles in severe, intractable VCD refractory to behavioral speech retraining.
mcq_angles: Flow-volume loop characteristics of VCD: truncated/flattened inspiratory loop with preserved expiratory loop (variable extrathoracic obstruction).
Gold standard diagnostic test: direct flexible nasolaryngoscopy demonstrating paradoxical vocal fold adduction during inspiration.
First-line therapy for VCD: speech therapy and respiratory retraining breathing maneuvers rather than bronchodilators or steroids.
case_hooks: A 17-year-old female competitive cross-country runner experiences acute severe breathlessness and high-pitched inspiratory wheezing that develops precisely 5 minutes into maximal sprinting and resolves 10 minutes post-rest; albuterol inhalers provide no relief.

A 42-year-old woman treated for 'refractory severe asthma' on triple-therapy inhalers and oral prednisone undergoes spirometry; the flow-volume loop shows complete flattening of the inspiratory loop with normal FEV1/FVC ratio.

page.mentor_intro: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome is an autosomal dominant hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome caused by germline inactivating mutations in the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p25.3. Loss of functional pVHL impairs ubiquitin-mediated degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor alpha (HIF-1alpha and HIF-2alpha), causing constitutive HIF accumulation and overtranscription of angiogenic and oncogenic target genes (VEGF, PDGF, erythropoietin). VHL manifests with multi-organ hypervascular neoplasms: central nervous system and retinal hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (pNETs).

teaching_points.claim: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion with high penetrance, caused by mutations in the VHL gene on chromosome 3p25, predisposing to hypervascular tumours driven by constitutive HIF-2alpha accumulation.

Surveillance for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) utilizes contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI/CT; to preserve long-term renal function, surgical intervention (nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy or thermal ablation) is deferred until the largest solid renal mass reaches 3 cm in diameter ('the 3 cm rule').

Pheochromocytomas in VHL produce predominantly normetanephrine (noradrenaline hypersecretion) rather than metanephrine/adrenaline; cortical-sparing partial adrenalectomy is preferred over total adrenalectomy to avoid lifelong adrenal insufficiency in bilateral disease.

Belzutifan—a first-in-class small-molecule oral HIF-2alpha inhibitor—is FDA/EMA approved for adult patients with VHL syndrome who require therapy for associated ccRCC, CNS hemangioblastomas, or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours not requiring immediate surgery, achieving high objective response rates (>50-60%).

uncertainties: Optimal duration of belzutifan therapy and safety of drug holidays in patients achieving durable objective radiographic tumor regression.
Malignant potential and surgical intervention thresholds for VHL-associated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours based on exon 3 mutations or size criteria (>2-3 cm).
mcq_angles: The '3 cm rule' for renal cell carcinoma in VHL: active surveillance for tumors <3 cm to preserve renal parenchyma and defer partial nephrectomy until >=3 cm.
Mechanism of action and indications for belzutifan: direct oral inhibitor of hypoxia-inducible factor-2alpha (HIF-2alpha) in VHL-associated neoplasms.
Screening guidelines: annual blood pressure and fractionated plasma/urinary metanephrines starting at age 5; biennial central nervous system and abdominal MRI starting in adolescence.
case_hooks: A 28-year-old male with known VHL syndrome has multiple bilateral renal cysts and a 2.4 cm solid enhancing cortex lesion in the right kidney on surveillance MRI; his eGFR is normal; the urologist recommends continued surveillance until the mass reaches 3 cm.
A 34-year-old female with VHL and growing multiple spinal hemangioblastomas and a 2.5 cm pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is initiated on oral belzutifan 120 mg daily.

page.mentor_intro: Von Willebrand Disease (VWD) is the most prevalent inherited human bleeding disorder, caused by quantitative deficiency or qualitative structural dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF serves dual critical hemostatic roles: mediating platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen at sites of vascular injury (via platelet glycoprotein Ib receptors) and serving as the carrier chaperone protein protecting circulating Factor VIII from rapid degradation. VWD is categorized into quantitative deficiencies (Type 1: partial deficiency, >75-80% of cases; Type 3: total absence) and qualitative structural defects (Type 2 variants: 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N), with treatment tailored to subtype and bleeding severity.

teaching_points.claim: VWD diagnostic evaluation requires a diagnostic panel: VWF antigen (VWF:Ag, quantitative level), VWF platelet-dependent activity (VWF:RCo or VWF:GPIbM / VWF:GPIbR, functional activity), Factor VIII coagulant activity (FVIII:C), and VWF multimers.

Type 1 VWD is characterized by proportional reduction of both VWF:Ag and VWF activity (VWF activity-to-antigen ratio >0.7); Type 2 variants exhibit qualitative defects with disproportionate functional loss (VWF activity-to-antigen ratio <0.7).

Desmopressin (DDAVP, 0.3 ug/kg IV or subcutaneous, or 300 ug concentrated nasal spray) stimulates rapid endogenous release of stored VWF and Factor VIII from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies; it is the first-line treatment for minor bleeding or procedural prophylaxis in Type 1 VWD.

Desmopressin is strictly contraindicated in Type 2B VWD because the mutant VWF has hyper-affinity for platelet GPIb receptors, causing platelet hyper-aggregation and precipitating acute severe thrombocytopenia; desmopressin is also ineffective in Type 3 VWD (no endogenous stores).

Plasma-derived or recombinant VWF concentrates containing Factor VIII are the definitive treatment for Type 3 VWD, severe Type 2 variants, and Type 1 patients unresponsive to or with contraindications to DDAVP.

uncertainties: Diagnostic definition and clinical bleeding significance of 'low VWF' levels (30-50 IU/dL) versus definitive VWD (<30 IU/dL).
Long-term efficacy and safety of recombinant VWF (vonicog alfa) compared to plasma-derived concentrates in major surgery and delivery.
mcq_angles: Contraindication of desmopressin (DDAVP) in Type 2B VWD: induces paradoxical platelet clumping and severe thrombocytopenia.
Distinguishing Type 1 (concordant ratio >0.7) from Type 2 variants (discordant activity/antigen ratio <0.7).
Type 2N VWD mimicry: qualitative defect in Factor VIII binding domain that mimics mild-to-moderate Haemophilia A in males and females.
case_hooks: A 22-year-old woman with severe menorrhagia and recurrent epistaxis has VWF:Ag 28%, VWF:RCo 24% (ratio 0.85), and FVIII 45%; a desmopressin trial demonstrates an excellent 3-fold rise in both VWF and FVIII.
A 14-year-old boy diagnosed with atypical VWD receives DDAVP prior to dental extraction; 1 hour post-dose, his platelet count drops precipitously from 180 to 22 x 10^9/L, confirming Type 2B VWD.

page.mentor_intro: V/Q Mismatch and pulmonary gas exchange is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

teaching_points.claim: Contemporary evidence synthesis highlights core pathophysiology, clinical staging, and multidisciplinary management: Pulmonary Embolism and Gas Exchange.

Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxemia in clinical medicine (e.g. COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, interstitial lung disease) and is characterized by an elevated alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient that corrects with low-to-moderate supplemental oxygen (FiO2 0.3-0.5).

True right-to-left anatomical or physiological shunt (V/Q ratio of zero, seen in severe ARDS, dense lobar consolidation, and intracardiac shunts) presents with refractory hypoxemia that does not fully correct even with 100% inspired oxygen.
Dead-space ventilation (V/Q ratio approaching infinity, seen in pulmonary embolism) impairs carbon dioxide elimination, resulting in hypercapnia and increased minute ventilation requirements.

page.mentor_intro: Critically ill, mechanically ventilated patients are at exceptionally high risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE) due to immobilization, vascular stasis, systemic inflammation, and invasive central venous access. Pharmacological thromboprophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin is the standard of care unless contraindicated by active hemorrhage.

teaching_points.claim: All critically ill mechanically ventilated adults require routine venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis; low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin 40 mg once daily or dalteparin 5,000 units once daily) is preferred over unfractionated heparin due to superior efficacy in reducing deep vein thrombosis and a lower incidence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).

In patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min), unfractionated heparin (5,000 units subcutaneously twice or three times daily) or dose-adjusted enoxaparin (20-30 mg once daily with anti-Xa monitoring) is recommended to avoid bioaccumulation and major bleeding.

Mechanical thromboprophylaxis with intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) devices is recommended in patients with active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia (platelets <50 x 10^9/L), or high bleeding risk until pharmacological anticoagulation can be safely introduced.

Routine surveillance venous Doppler ultrasonography is not recommended in asymptomatic ICU patients; however, sudden unexplained hypoxemia, tachycardia, right ventricular strain, or acute difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation mandates urgent evaluation for pulmonary embolism.

uncertainties: Benefit of weight-adjusted or anti-Xa-guided LMWH dosing versus standard fixed dosing in morbidly obese critically ill patients.
Role of extended post-ICU pharmacological thromboprophylaxis in patients with persistent severe mobility impairment.
mcq_angles: LMWH versus UFH in critical care: LMWH significantly reduces DVT and pulmonary embolism risk with lower rates of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
Management of active coagulopathy: mechanical prophylaxis (IPC) alone until active hemorrhage resolves, followed by prompt resumption of LMWH.
Renal adjustment rules: enoxaparin accumulates in renal failure; switch to UFH or reduce dose to 30 mg daily with peak anti-Xa level monitoring (target 0.2-0.5 IU/mL).

page.mentor_intro: Nephrotic syndrome—defined by heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/24h), hypoalbuminaemia (<30 g/L), peripheral oedema, and hypercholesterolaemia—is a potent prothrombotic state. The hypercoagulable state is driven by urinary loss of natural anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin III, protein S), enhanced hepatic synthesis of procoagulant factors (fibrinogen, factor V, factor VIII), thrombocytosis, platelet hyper-reactivity, and hemoconcentration. Venous thromboembolism (VTE) occurs in up to 10-40% of adult nephrotic patients—most prominently renal vein thrombosis (RVT), deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism; membranous nephropathy carries the highest thrombotic risk, warranting individualized prophylactic anticoagulation.

teaching_points.claim: The risk of venous thromboembolism in nephrotic syndrome is inversely proportional to serum albumin; thrombosis risk rises steeply when serum albumin falls below 20-25 g/L (2.0-2.5 g/dL), particularly in membranous nephropathy.

Membranous nephropathy (MN) carries the highest incidence of VTE and renal vein thrombosis among all causes of nephrotic syndrome; KDIGO guidelines recommend prophylactic anticoagulation in MN patients with serum albumin <20-25 g/L and additional thrombotic risk factors.

Renal vein thrombosis (RVT) presents either insidiously or acutely with severe flank pain, gross haematuria, rapid decline in renal function, and sudden worsening of proteinuria; Doppler ultrasound or contrast CT venography provides definitive diagnosis.

Warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban) are effective for VTE prophylaxis; however, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) and unfractionated heparin rely on antithrombin III, which is significantly depleted in severe nephrotic proteinuria, potentially requiring higher doses or direct factor Xa inhibitors.

uncertainties: Safety and efficacy of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban) compared to warfarin for primary VTE prophylaxis in nephrotic patients with severe hypoalbuminaemia.
Exact bleeding versus thrombotic risk score cutoffs to guide prophylactic anticoagulation duration during immunosuppressive induction.
mcq_angles: Identifying serum albumin thresholds (<20-25 g/L) and histological subtype (membranous nephropathy) that trigger consideration of prophylactic anticoagulation.
Clinical presentation of acute renal vein thrombosis: sudden flank pain, macroscopic haematuria, and acute renal decline.
Pharmacologic considerations: why heparin efficacy may be blunted by urinary antithrombin III loss, favoring DOACs or adjusted LMWH.

page.mentor_intro: Vulvar and vaginal cancers are rare gynaecological malignancies predominantly comprising squamous cell carcinomas (SCC, >80-90%). Pathogenesis follows dual distinct etiologic pathways: human papillomavirus (HPV)-dependent pathways (associated with high-risk HPV types 16 and 18, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions [HSIL / vVIN], younger patients, and smoking) and HPV-independent pathways (associated with chronic inflammatory lichen sclerosus, differentiated VIN [dVIN], TP53 mutations, and older age). Treatment centers on individualised radical wide local excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) or inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy, followed by adjuvant chemoradiotherapy for positive nodal metastasis.

teaching_points.claim: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma arises via two distinct carcinogenic pathways: HPV-associated (younger women, p16 positive, better prognosis) and HPV-independent (older women, associated with lichen sclerosus, TP53 mutated, higher recurrence rates).

Inguinofemoral lymph node status is the single most critical prognostic determinant for survival; sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) using radiotracer and blue dye or indocyanine green is the standard of care for unifocal tumours <4 cm without clinically suspicious groin nodes (GROINSS-V trials).

Surgical management of early vulvar cancer requires radical local excision achieving >=1 cm gross surgical margins (histological clearance >=8 mm after tissue fixation) to minimize local recurrence risk while avoiding disfiguring radical vulvectomy.

Primary vaginal cancer is rare (most vaginal malignancies represent metastases from cervix, vulva, or endometrium); definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (external beam radiation plus brachytherapy with cisplatin) is the standard of care for locally advanced (Stage II-IV) primary vaginal carcinoma.

uncertainties: Safety of omitting full inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy in patients with isolated micrometastases (<=2 mm) detected on sentinel lymph node biopsy (GROINSS-V II trial).
Efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab) in recurrent or metastatic HPV-associated versus HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma.
mcq_angles: Prognostic importance of inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy / SLNB in vulvar cancer staging and management.
Dual pathways of vulvar carcinogenesis: p16/HPV-associated vs p53/lichen sclerosus-associated.
Primary treatment modality for locally advanced vaginal cancer: definitive chemoradiotherapy with image-guided brachytherapy rather than radical exenterative surgery.

page.mentor_intro: Walled-Off Pancreatic Necrosis (WON) is a mature, encapsulated collection of solid pancreatic and/or peripancreatic necrotic tissue enclosed by a thick inflammatory wall, typically developing >=4 weeks after the onset of acute necrotizing pancreatitis. Differentiating sterile from infected necrosis is the crucial clinical junction: infected necrosis—confirmed by new fevers, leukocytosis, sepsis, or presence of gas bubbles on contrast-enhanced CT—is a life-threatening indication for intervention. The international standard of care has definitively shifted from open surgical necrosectomy to the minimally invasive 'step-up approach' (conservative medical therapy and antibiotics, followed by endoscopic or percutaneous catheter drainage, and endoscopic transmural necrosectomy only when needed).

teaching_points.claim: Walled-off pancreatic necrosis (WON) is distinguished from pancreatic pseudocyst by containing solid necrotic debris on contrast-enhanced CT or endoscopic ultrasound (pseudocysts contain pure non-necrotic amylase-rich fluid); draining WON requires wide-caliber access to evacuate solid necrosis.

The minimally invasive step-up approach (PANTER trial) is the standard of care for infected necrotizing pancreatitis, reducing new-onset organ failure, long-term complications (pancreatic insufficiency, incisional hernias), and healthcare costs compared to primary open surgical necrosectomy.

Endoscopic step-up approach utilizing endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided transmural drainage with lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS, e.g., Axios) followed by direct endoscopic necrosectomy (DEN) as needed demonstrates equivalent mortality with significantly lower fistula rates and hospital stay compared to surgical step-up drainage (TENSION trial).

Intervention should be delayed whenever clinically feasible until >=4 weeks from pancreatitis onset, allowing the necrotic collection to organize and form a mature fibrous encapsulation ('walling-off'), which dramatically reduces procedural bleeding and perforation risks.

uncertainties: Optimal timing for removing lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS) (typically 3-4 weeks) to prevent delayed pseudoaneurysm bleeding from stent erosion into adjacent splenic or gastroduodenal vessels.
Role of upfront direct endoscopic necrosectomy (DEN) at the index drainage procedure versus a true staged step-up drainage-first protocol (DESTIN trial).
mcq_angles: PANTER and TENSION trial outcomes: superiority of the minimally invasive endoscopic step-up approach over open necrosectomy.
Timing of intervention: intentionally delaying intervention to >=4 weeks post-onset to allow mature fibrous wall formation.
Differentiating pancreatic pseudocyst from walled-off necrosis on imaging (solid necrotic tissue vs homogeneous fluid).
case_hooks: A 48-year-old male 5 weeks post-severe acute gallstone pancreatitis develops spiking fevers and leukocytosis; CT abdomen reveals a 12 cm retroperitoneal encapsulated collection containing mixed fluid, non-enhancing solid debris, and multiple gas pockets (infected WON).

An interventional endoscopist performs EUS-guided cystogastrostomy using a 20 mm lumen-apposing metal stent (LAMS) into a mature retroperitoneal WON collection, evacuating 800 mL of purulent necrotic debris.

page.mentor_intro: Wellens syndrome is a pain-free ECG pattern of proximal LAD stenosis; diffuse ST depression with ST elevation in aVR suggests left main or multivessel disease. Both need early angiography.

teaching_points.claim: Wellens syndrome shows biphasic (type A, about 25%) or deeply inverted symmetric (type B, about 75%) T waves in V2 to V3 during pain-free periods, with no significant ST elevation or Q waves.
It indicates critical proximal LAD stenosis with high risk of anterior infarction; urgent angiography is needed and exercise stress testing is contraindicated.
Diffuse ST depression in 6 or more leads with ST elevation in aVR (and sometimes V1) suggests left main or severe multivessel disease and calls for emergency cardiology review and angiography.
In those patients management follows the NSTE-ACS pathway with antithrombotic therapy, but immediate angiography is warranted when haemodynamically unstable.

page.mentor_intro: Withdrawal syndrome encompasses the cluster of physiological and psychological signs and symptoms that emerge upon abrupt cessation, rapid dose reduction, or antagonist administration of a drug or substance of dependence. Underlying mechanisms reflect neuroadaptation: chronic receptor activation or inhibition triggers compensatory changes in neurotransmitter receptors and second-messenger cascades. Withdrawal syndromes range from benign and uncomfortable (opioid, nicotine, cannabis withdrawal) to acute, potentially fatal medical emergencies—most prominently alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal syndromes—which cause severe autonomic hyperarousal, seizures, and delirium tremens.

teaching_points.claim: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome is a medical emergency caused by down-regulated inhibitory GABA-A receptors and upregulated excitatory NMDA receptors; symptoms progress from autonomic hyperactivity (tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia) at 6-24 hours, to withdrawal seizures at 12-48 hours, and delirium tremens (confusion, severe agitation, visual hallucinations, autonomic instability) at 48-96 hours.

Validated symptom-triggered therapy using the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA-Ar) protocol with long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam or chlordiazepoxide) is the standard of care, significantly reducing total benzodiazepine requirements and hospital stay compared to fixed-schedule dosing.

In patients with severe hepatic cirrhosis or advanced age, short- or intermediate-acting benzodiazepines without active hepatic metabolites (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam—remembered by 'LOT') are preferred to avoid prolonged drug accumulation and oversedation.

Phenobarbital (long-acting barbiturate enhancing GABA-A receptor opening duration and directly inhibiting AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors) is an increasingly utilized, highly effective protocolized alternative to benzodiazepines for severe alcohol withdrawal in emergency and ICU settings.

Opioid withdrawal (dysphoria, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, piloerection, pupillary dilation, severe myalgias) is intensely distressing but rarely life-threatening in adults; management utilizes alpha-2 adrenergic agonists (clonidine, lofexidine) for autonomic symptoms, or buprenorphine/methadone substitution tapering.

uncertainties: Single-dose or front-loaded intravenous phenobarbital versus standard symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocols for ICU admission avoidance in acute alcohol withdrawal.
Optimal tapering strategies and risk of persistent post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS) in patients discontinuing long-term therapeutic benzodiazepines or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
mcq_angles: Selecting benzodiazepines in alcohol withdrawal with severe liver disease: utilizing lorazepam or oxazepam ('LOT' agents that undergo direct glucuronidation without CYP metabolism).
Delirium tremens timing and hallmarks: onset at 48-96 hours, characterized by delirium, autonomic instability, and visual hallucinations.
Phenobarbital pharmacology: dual mechanism (GABA-A enhancement and AMPA receptor inhibition) providing stable self-tapering anticonvulsant sedation.

page.mentor_intro: Wolfram syndrome is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder from WFS1 mutations, presenting with diabetes mellitus and optic atrophy, later diabetes insipidus, deafness, and neurological and urinary problems. Care is supportive.

teaching_points.claim: Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) is usually caused by recessive WFS1 mutations; childhood-onset non-autoimmune insulin-requiring diabetes is typically first, followed by optic atrophy, central diabetes insipidus and sensorineural deafness.

Management is supportive: insulin, desmopressin, hearing aids or cochlear implant, visual aids, and bladder care; there is no disease-modifying treatment.
Surveillance covers ophthalmology, audiometry, urodynamics and renal ultrasound, plus neurological follow-up.

teaching_points.claim: Clinical practice guideline consensus establishes evidence-directed diagnostic criteria and risk-stratified therapy for workup for new heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice and Multi-Society Consensus on workup for new heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

Comprehensive diagnostic evaluation of newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) requires comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography, laboratory evaluation (NT-proBNP, complete blood count, renal and liver function, thyroid stimulating hormone, ferritin and transferrin saturation to detect iron deficiency), and non-invasive or invasive coronary angiography to exclude ischemic heart disease, alongside cardiac MRI when non-ischemic cardiomyopathy or myocarditis is suspected.

Iron deficiency (ferritin <100 ug/L, or 100-299 ug/L with TSAT <20%) occurs in up to 50% of HFrEF patients; intravenous ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose improves symptoms, quality of life, and reduces heart failure hospitalizations.

Guideline-directed medical therapy with the four foundational pillar drug classes (ARNI/ACEi, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor) should be initiated and uptitrated promptly to reduce cardiovascular mortality.

page.mentor_intro: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is a clinical syndrome caused by severe, unregulated hypersecretion of gastric acid driven by autonomous gastrin release from a neuroendocrine tumour (gastrinoma). Gastrinomas are located primarily within the 'gastrinoma triangle' (bounded by the confluence of the cystic/common bile duct, junction of the 2nd/3rd duodenal parts, and neck/body of the pancreas), occurring sporadically (75-80%) or as part of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1, 20-25%). Clinical hallmarks include severe, recurrent, refractory peptic ulcer disease (often in atypical locations like the distal duodenum or jejunum), severe reflux oesophagitis, and chronic watery secretory diarrhoea that resolves with gastric acid suppression.

teaching_points.claim: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome should be suspected in patients with multiple peptic ulcers, ulcers in atypical post-bulbar or jejunal locations, ulcers refractory to standard therapy, ulcers associated with severe chronic diarrhea, or personal/family history of MEN1 endocrinopathies.

Initial diagnostic screening requires measuring fasting serum gastrin (FSG); an FSG >1000 pg/mL (>10-fold ULN) in the presence of gastric acid hypersecretion (gastric pH <=2.0) is virtually pathognomonic for ZES.

Prior to measuring fasting serum gastrin, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) must be temporarily discontinued for at least 1-2 weeks (with bridging via H2-receptor antagonists, held 24-48 hours before testing), as PPI-induced hypochlorhydria causes secondary physiological hypergastrinaemia that generates false-positive results.

If fasting serum gastrin is non-diagnostic (between 100 and 1000 pg/mL with pH <=2), a secretin stimulation test is the confirmatory test of choice; a paradoxical rise in serum gastrin of >120 pg/mL above baseline confirms ZES.

Primary tumor localization is established with 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT (somatostatin receptor imaging), which possesses superior sensitivity (>90%) over conventional CT/MRI and octreotide scintigraphy; high-dose PPI therapy (e.g., omeprazole 60-120 mg daily) is the medical treatment of choice to control acid hypersecretion.

uncertainties: Surgical resection versus conservative medical surveillance in patients with MEN1-associated multifocal duodenal microgastrinomas.
Role of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT with 177Lu-DOTATATE) in metastatic, unresectable gastrinomas progressing on somatostatin analogues.

page.gaps: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.
